result.summary: The HELIX Lite sketch is fundamentally sound for its goals (SSA scalar opts, affine dependence analysis, Cranelift JIT), but it is underspecified in roughly a dozen places that will cause rework during typechecking and codegen if frozen as-is. Recommended freeze: zero implicit coercions (with one pragmatic exception — array-index widening to i64), i64 as the sole arithmetic integer with i32 as a storage-only array element type, mandatory braces (kills dangling-else), ranges restricted to for-headers only, checked-by-default semantics (bounds, div-by-zero) implemented as explicit guarded branches rather than native faults, and a 7-builtin stdlib (print, zeros, len, abs, sqrt, min, max) that covers matmul/Mandelbrot/N-body/sieve/reduction demos. Cranelift maps cleanly onto these choices: `%` is srem (sign of dividend), `/` is sdiv (traps /0 and INT_MIN/-1), float-to-int casts use fcvt_to_int_sat semantics (NaN→0, saturate), and sqrt/fabs are first-class instructions. Pin one cranelift crate family (current line ~0.135.x, Aug 2026) since wasmtime ships several majors in lockstep.
key_facts: Cranelift version landscape (verified Aug 2026): cranelift-jit newest_version 0.123.14 on an older maintained train but max_stable_version 0.135.0 (last publish 2026-08-20); docs.rs currently documents cranelift-frontend 0.134.3; wasmtime shows newest_version 36.0.14 vs max_stable_version 48.0.0 — multiple release trains ship in parallel, so pin an exact minor family (e.g. cranelift = "0.135") rather than a loose caret.

cranelift-frontend API surface confirmed current and non-deprecated: FunctionBuilder (declare_var/def_var/use_var), FunctionBuilderContext, Variable — Variable-based mutable variables are auto-converted to SSA, which exactly matches HELIX's 'mutable scalars via reassignment' model; Switch struct exists for later switch lowering.

Cranelift sdiv traps on divisor==zero AND on INT_MIN/-1 ('result not representable'); it is formally a cannot-speculate trapping instruction (IntDivTrap::{Zero,Overflow} in codegen/src/ir/instructions.rs). On x64 idiv faults natively; on AArch64 Cranelift inserts explicit guard branches.

Cranelift srem is truncated remainder: result has the SIGN OF THE DIVIDEND (matches C/Rust % and Python's // pairing), undefined for /0 and INT_MIN/-1. smod is floored modulo with sign of the DIVISOR (Python % style). HELIX '%' should be specced as srem semantics: -7 % 2 == -1, 7 % -2 == 1.

Cranelift fmin/fmax are specified IEEE 754-2008 minNum/maxNum: if exactly one operand is NaN, return the OTHER operand; NaN only if both are NaN. Known implementation hazard rust-lang/rust#9903: naive lowering via x86 MINSS/MAXSS propagates NaN from either operand. Relevant if HELIX min/max builtins or reductions are lowered to fmin/fmax — verify or use select(fcmp ord)-style sequences.

fcvt_to_int_sat / fcvt_to_uint_sat (i32/i64 variants): NaN becomes 0, out-of-range saturates to MIN/MAX incl. infinities — identical to Rust's `as` cast semantics standardized in Rust 1.45 (RFC 2535). Non-saturating fcvt_to_int is UB when the value does not fit. Use the _sat forms so interpreter and JIT agree bit-for-bit.

sqrt.f32/.f64 is a first-class deterministic IEEE instruction (NaN for negative input); fabs and copysign are bitwise-sign instructions. There is NO pow/exp/log instruction in Cranelift — anything beyond sqrt must come from libm FFI or polynomial demos.

Bounds/div-zero strategy constraint: cranelift-jit is officially 'not intended for production yet'; Windows x64 IS a supported ISA target, and the historic >2GB VirtualAlloc(MEM_COMMIT) limitation on Windows was fixed via MEM_RESERVE (wasmtime issue #523), but relying on native divide faults for language-level errors means catching them through Windows SEH/vectored exception handlers — fragile under a JIT. Explicit compare-and-call-panic-guard codegen is portable and teachable.

Rust precedent worth citing in the reference appendix: float->int `as` casts round toward zero, NaN->0, saturation at type limits (doc.rust-lang.org/reference, 'numeric cast'); Rust `%` is truncated remainder matching Cranelift srem; Rust requires braces and has no dangling-else, which is the style HELIX should copy.
recommendations: BUILTINS — freeze exactly 7: print(e) (any scalar, or [T] printed as '[v0, v1, ...]' on one line; returns unit); zeros(n) -> [T] with element type inferred from the annotated binding (requires `let a: [f64] = zeros(n);`); len(a) -> i64; abs(x) (same numeric type back); sqrt(x) (f32->f32, f64->f64, negative input = NaN per IEEE); min(a,b)/max(a,b) (same-type numerics, IEEE minNum/maxNum NaN rule: non-NaN wins). Nothing else. This set runs matmul, Mandelbrot (iteration counts, no math builtins needed), N-body (sqrt), prime sieve (zeros+[bool]), dot-product/reduction parallelization showcases, and histograms — the smallest set that demos beautifully. Deliberately exclude: pow/exp/log (no Cranelift instruction; would force libm FFI plumbing), floor/ceil, string formatting, input(), a separate println (print always appends newline).

GRAMMAR — adopt the EBNF below verbatim. Key closure decisions: (1) comments // to end-of-line and /* */ block comments, NON-nested (C-style; note divergence from Rust explicitly); (2) unary ops are - and !, binding tighter than * / %; (3) six precedence levels, all binary left-associative: || < && < == != < < > <= >= < + - < * / % < unary < postfix(index/call) < primary; `as` casts bind tighter than unary minus (-x as i32 parses as -(x as i32)); parentheses group; (4) && and || SHORT-CIRCUIT mandatorily and desugar to branch diamonds in your CFG IR — this is a selling-point exercise, not overhead; (5) ranges appear ONLY in for headers: `for i in e1..e2` half-open [e1,e2), no step clause in v1 (reserve keyword `by`; add strided form only when a tiling demo actually needs it), no `..=` inclusive form, ranges are NOT first-class values; (6) else-if chains fall out of `else (if-stmt | block)` recursion; BRACES MANDATORY on every if/for body — eliminates dangling-else by construction; (7) nested functions DISALLOWED (flat global function table, trivial name resolution); recursion ALLOWED (fib/factorial demos; free via native Cranelift call lowering); multiple return values NO; early return YES — lowers to a branch on a dedicated exit block holding the single return value, a clean SSA/phi lesson; (8) assignment is a STATEMENT, not an expression — kills `a=b=c` and the `if x=y` typo class; (9) reserve now, implement later: while, break, continue, mut, in, as (used), true/false (used), and, or, not, struct, import.

TYPES — zero implicit coercions between int and float; the ONLY sanctioned implicit conversion is array INDEX i32->i64 widening (students write `a[i]` with i32 counters constantly; forcing `as` there poisons ergonomics for no pedagogical gain). Integers: make i64 the one arithmetic integer — unannotated integer literals infer i64; i32 exists purely as an array element/storage type for cache-bandwidth demos; mixing i32 and i64 VALUES in an operator requires an explicit `as` cast. Evaluate-and-reject alternative: automatic i32->i64 promotion everywhere — it doubles the checker rules and the number of Cranelift value types you juggle for zero demo benefit. Bool: NO truthiness, conditions must be typed bool, no int<->bool coercion, `!` is the only bool op besides comparisons. Arrays: element types must match exactly for assignment/passing; arrays are fat pointers (base+len), passed by REFERENCE so callee writes escape (write this sentence into the spec verbatim — it is the load-bearing semantic for your escape demos); arrays are not copyable; NESTED ARRAYS FORBIDDEN in v1 ([T] where T is scalar only) — flat arrays keep subscript analysis affine and LICM sound; matrices are done with manual r*n+c indexing (good for the dependence-analysis narrative). Unit type: spelled (), procedures are `fn f(...)` with no arrow or `-> ()`; calling a unit function inside an expression is a static error; `return;` vs `return expr;` distinguished by declared return type.

SEMANTICS — freeze these five policies: (1) integer / and % by zero AND i64::MIN / -1 or % -1 are RUNTIME ERRORS with a source-location message in the interpreter; in JIT codegen emit an explicit guard (compare divisor to 0, branch to a panic stub) before sdiv/srem — do NOT rely on native x86 #DE faults, because converting those into clean errors under cranelift-jit on Windows means fighting SEH/vectored handlers; one extra branch per division is negligible and portable. (2) Signed integer OVERFLOW elsewhere is defined two's-complement WRAPPING (document it; consistent with choosing not to trap on abs(i64::MIN), which should also wrap). (3) Floats are full IEEE: NaN and +/-Inf flow through arithmetic, float division by zero produces Inf/NaN (never traps), print renders 'nan'/'inf'. (4) Array bounds are CHECKED BY DEFAULT in both interpreter and JIT (same compare-and-trap pattern); provide --unchecked to strip checks for perf-comparison benchmarks and state plainly that OOB access under --unchecked is UB and may crash. This checked-vs-unchecked delta is itself a great lab measurement of safety cost. (5) DEFINITE ASSIGNMENT is enforced statically by a dataflow pass (every variable initialized on all paths to a use; arrays come pre-initialized from zeros) — it doubles as the warm-up for your liveness/DCE passes. Out-parameter convention: NONE — one return value plus array-reference mutation is the only multi-output idiom (write results into a caller-supplied output array).

ENTRY POINT — require exactly one `fn main()` with zero parameters returning unit; the driver looks it up in the function table and errors if missing/duplicated. PROGRAM-LEVEL STATEMENTS FORBIDDEN: the top level contains only fn definitions and optionally `const NAME: type = literal;` scalar constants (useful for shared problem sizes like `const N: i64 = 1024;`; forbid const arrays in v1). This keeps the module layout = a flat symbol table, which is all Cranelift's Module/JITBuilder needs anyway (one cranelift_function per fn, main invoked through a typed function pointer signature () -> ()).

PARALLELIZATION-FACING SPEC SENTENCES (write them now so the language reference and the optimizer chapter stay consistent): (a) for-loop bodies must not reassign the loop variable (statically rejected) — guarantees affine iteration space; (b) print is a side effect and a loop containing print is never parallelized — otherwise parallel output ordering destroys demo credibility; (c) passing the SAME array variable as two arguments of one call (f(a, a)) is statically rejected — cheap syntactic check that protects your loop-carried-dependence analysis from aliasing it cannot see; (d) reductions recognized for +, -, *, min, max accumulate into a single scalar accumulator matching the canonical `acc = acc op a[i]` shape.

PROPOSED EBNF (freeze-ready, sized for the appendix): program ::= { fn_def | const_def }; fn_def ::= 'fn' IDENT '(' [param {',' param}] ')' ['->' type] block; const_def ::= 'const' IDENT ':' type '=' literal ';'; param ::= IDENT ':' type; type ::= 'i32'|'i64'|'f32'|'f64'|'bool'|'[' scalar_type ']'|'()' ; scalar_type ::= 'i32'|'i64'|'f32'|'f64'|'bool'; block ::= '{' {stmt} '}'; stmt ::= let_stmt | assign_stmt | if_stmt | for_stmt | return_stmt | expr ';' | ';' | block; let_stmt ::= 'let' IDENT [':' type] '=' expr ';'; assign_stmt ::= lvalue '=' expr ';'; lvalue ::= IDENT ['[' expr ']']; if_stmt ::= 'if' expr block {'else' (if_stmt | block)}; for_stmt ::= 'for' IDENT 'in' expr '..' expr block; return_stmt ::= 'return' [expr] ';'; expr ::= or_expr; or_expr ::= and_expr {'||' and_expr}; and_expr ::= eq_expr {'&&' eq_expr}; eq_expr ::= rel_expr {('=='|'!=') rel_expr}; rel_expr ::= add_expr {('<'|'>'|'<='|'>=') add_expr}; add_expr ::= mul_expr {('+'|'-') mul_expr}; mul_expr ::= unary_expr {('*'|'/'|'%') unary_expr}; unary_expr ::= ('-'|'!') unary_expr | cast_expr; cast_expr ::= postfix {'as' scalar_type}; postfix ::= primary ['[' expr ']'] | primary ['(' [expr {',' expr}] ')']; primary ::= literal | IDENT | '(' expr ')'; literal ::= INT_LIT | FLOAT_LIT | 'true' | 'false'. Lexer: comment ::= '//' {!NEWLINE} | '/*' {!'*/'} '*/' (non-nested).

TYPE-RULE TABLE (appendix-ready): arith +,-,* : both operands same numeric type -> that type; / : ints -> same int type, traps /0 and INT_MIN/-1; floats -> IEEE quotient; % : ints only, srem semantics (sign follows dividend), traps same as /; unary - : numeric -> same; comparisons < > <= >= : same numeric type -> bool; == != : same scalar type -> bool (arrays NOT comparable); && || : bool,bool short-circuit -> bool; ! : bool -> bool; a[i] : a:[T], i:i32-or-i64 (widened to i64) -> T, bounds-checked; f(args) : exact parameter types (index-widening excepted) -> declared return type; x as T : numeric->numeric only (bool excluded, arrays excluded), fcvt_to_int_sat semantics for float->int (NaN->0, saturate); zeros(n) : n:i64 (or i32 widened) -> [T], T from annotation; len(a) : a:[T] -> i64; print(e) : any -> ().
pitfalls: Relying on native divide faults (x86 #DE) for div-by-zero errors: under cranelift-jit on Windows this surfaces as an OS exception needing vectored exception handling to report cleanly — fragile and platform-specific. Always emit explicit compare-and-branch guards to a panic stub, uniformly for div-by-zero, INT_MIN/-1, and bounds checks.

% sign confusion: Cranelift srem (HELIX '%') follows the DIVIDEND's sign (-7 % 2 == -1) while students arriving from Python expect floored modulo (-7 % 2 == 1). Put a worked example in the reference or this generates bug reports all semester. Do not be tempted to expose smod too.

If you lower min/max builtins or reductions straight to Cranelift fmin/fmax, remember the documented IEEE minNum/maxNum contract (non-NaN operand wins) differs from what x86 MINSS/MAXSS naively produce (either-side NaN propagation) — the exact discrepancy behind rust-lang/rust#9903. Test min/max with NaN inputs, or build them from select+ordered-compare.

Float->int casts must use saturating semantics (fcvt_to_int_sat: NaN->0, clamp at limits) in BOTH interpreter and JIT. Using plain fcvt_to_int is UB on out-of-range values and WILL diverge between your tree-walking interpreter and generated code — a nightmare debugging scenario in a course setting.

Version pinning: wasmtime/Cranelift publishes multiple major trains simultaneously (36.x patches shipping alongside 48.0.0 as of Aug 2026) and cranelift-jit is labeled experimental/'not intended for production'. Lock Cargo.toml to one exact 0.13x family and record it in the reference; blind caret upgrades can change legalization behavior mid-semester.

Implicit int->float coercion would quietly poison reduction recognition and dependence classification (int += is associative-integer-exact, float += is NOT associativity-safe) — one more reason the zero-coercion recommendation is load-bearing, not just aesthetic. If anyone re-litigates coercions, route them to the parallelization argument.

Nested arrays ([[T]]) or array copy-on-pass would break the flat affine subscript model and the 'writes escape' demos respectively. Freeze '[T] where T is scalar' and fat-pointer reference passing as non-negotiable; also reject duplicate-array-argument calls f(a, a) statically or your independence proof silently assumes away aliasing.

Allowing ranges as ordinary values (or a step/inclusive form) prematurely drags in a range type, iteration-protocol design, and heap allocation — none of which serve the optimization storyline. Restrict '..' syntactically to for headers; the grammar production above enforces it for free.
Braceless if/for bodies reintroduce the dangling-else ambiguity and special-case parser recovery for zero benefit. Mandatory braces (Rust/Go style) is the correct freeze.

print inside parallelizable loops: unless the spec states that side effects block parallelization, students will see scrambled output and conclude the parallelizer is broken. State it explicitly, and consider having the compiler PRINT a notice ('loop L not parallelized: contains side effect') — turns a pitfall into a feature demo.
Unit-returning functions used as expressions must be a hard type error; if tolerated, you get silent zero-values flowing through DCE and confusing optimizer traces.

Missing definite-assignment enforcement shows up as nondeterministic garbage in JIT runs that benchmarks 'great' — enforce it statically before any performance work, and reuse the pass as your liveness-analysis teaching example.
references: https://cranelift.readthedocs.io/en/latest/instruction-reference.html (sdiv/srem/smod trapping contracts; fmin/fmax NaN semantics; sqrt/fabs/copysign; fcvt_to_int_sat)
https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/issues/523 (Windows JIT >2GB VirtualAlloc limitation and MEM_RESERVE fix)
https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/operator-expr.html (numeric `as` cast semantics: round toward zero, NaN->0, saturation — precedent for HELIX cast rules)

result.summary: For HELIX Lite's "Observatory" visualization app with zero npm toolchain, the strongest 2026 stack is axum 0.8.x (actively maintained, 0.8.9 April 2026) serving ~5 embedded assets via include_bytes!/rust-embed 8.x bound to 127.0.0.1, with a vanilla-JS frontend that reuses HELIX's own lexer tokens for syntax highlighting and renders SVG directly. Vendor d3 v7.9.0 UMD (~280 KB) locally once for AST tidy-tree layout, and either hand-roll a layered CFG layout (~100 lines) or better yet compute CFG coordinates in Rust and ship them in the JSON so the browser is a dumb renderer. Hand-rolled SVG bar charts beat Chart.js for two benchmark charts (zero deps, full dark-theme control, CSS-transition animations). A ratatui 0.30.x TUI is a poor fit for CFGs (braille canvas caps resolution, no native graph widget) — keep the TUI as a bonus text-mode view, not the demo centerpiece; a hybrid CLI that auto-opens the browser on localhost is the impressive path.
key_facts: axum 0.8.9 released 2026-04-14, ~436M total downloads, published by Alice Ryhl (Tokio team) — actively maintained as of Aug 2026
warp 0.4.3 released 2026-05-04 (seanmonstar), ~46M downloads — maintained but filter-based API is clunkier for mixed JSON+static apps
tiny_http 0.12.0 last updated 2022-10-06 (~60M downloads) — lightest (no async runtime) but nearly 4 years without a release; you hand-roll routing, MIME types, and JSON responses
rust-embed 8.12.0 released 2026-07-08: reads files from disk in debug builds (live reload DX), embeds into binary in release builds; #[derive(RustEmbed)] #[folder = "dist/"]

axum SPA-without-tower-http pattern: Router::new().route("/api/...", get(handler)).fallback(get(|| async { Html(include_str!("index.html")) })); tower_http::ServeDir serves from filesystem only and CANNOT serve include_str!/include_bytes! data

d3 v7.9.0 is the latest v7: dist/d3.v7.min.js ~280 KB minified (~85 KB gzipped), UMD global `d3`; official d3js.org/getting-started offers direct downloads explicitly for offline use; the May 2026 GitHub PR claiming v7 went ESM-only (d3/d3#4125) was disputed and CLOSED — UMD remains fully supported

d3-hierarchy implements Buchheim et al. 2002 linear-time Reingold-Tilford tidy tree; layout is ~3 calls: const tree = d3.tree().nodeSize([40,120]); tree(d3.hierarchy(data)); then draw root.descendants()/root.links()

@dagrejs/dagre 3.1.1 ships dist/dagre.min.js UMD (~100 KB minified, MIT) attaching global `dagre`; maintenance resumed under the dagrejs org after years archived; Sugiyama-style layered layout ideal for CFGs

elkjs 0.12.0 ships lib/elk.bundled.js usable via <script> tag but it is ~1-2 MB (GWT-compiled Eclipse Layout Kernel) and dual-licensed EPL-2.0 OR GPL-3.0-or-later — heavier and less course-friendly than dagre
Chart.js: the npm package main entry is ESM and FAILS via plain <script> from file://; the correct offline file is dist/chart.umd.min.js (~200 KB min, self-contained, inlines @kurkle/color)

Prism.js core ~2 KB plus per-language definitions, registers custom grammars as plain objects (Prism.languages.x = {...}) with NO build step; highlight.js default bundle ~120 KB covering 190+ languages but custom grammars require module builds

ratatui 0.30.2 released 2026-06-19; Canvas widget draws points/lines/rectangles/circles via braille characters with no first-class node/edge concept; built-in BarChart is vertical-bars-only with no animation; no native graph widget exists (community ratatui-graph is experimental)

Minimal Reingold-Tilford implementations run 50-80 lines (recursive post-order x-assignment + subtree shifting); Bill Mill's llimllib.github.io/pymag-trees/ is the canonical walkthrough; Buchheim linear-time variant fixes Walker's O(n^2) worst case

Okabe-Ito colorblind-safe categorical hex values: Orange #E69F00, Sky Blue #56B4E9, Bluish Green #009E73, Yellow #F0E442, Blue #0072B2, Vermillion #D55E00, Reddish Purple #CC79A7; canonical citation Wong, Nature Methods 8:441 (2011)
WCAG 2.1 targets: >=4.5:1 contrast for text, >=3:1 for graphical objects; ~8% of males have red-green color deficiency so hue must never be the sole signal
One Dark Pro-derived syntax palette proven on dark backgrounds: keywords #c678dd, types/functions #56b6c2/#61afef, numbers #d19a66, strings #98c379, comments #5c6370, plain identifiers #abb2bf
recommendations: Serve with axum 0.8 behind a feature flag (`helix observe` subcommand): Router::new().route("/api/artifact", get(json_handler)).fallback(index_handler), binding 127.0.0.1:<port>, then auto-open the default browser via the `webbrowser` crate (or `cmd /c start` on Win11). Skip tower-http entirely — with <=6 assets you don't need ServeDir.

Embed assets with plain include_bytes! in a match-on-path fallback handler rather than adding rust-embed's proc-macro, UNLESS you want debug-build live reload — then rust-embed 8.12 is worth its one dependency (debug = disk, release = embedded). Set explicit Content-Type headers (.html/.css/.js/.svg); browsers ignore wrong MIME for scripts only in some cases — set them correctly.

Reuse YOUR OWN lexer as the syntax highlighter: the TOKENS phase already produces spans; emit `<span class="tok-kw">` etc. from those spans. Zero libraries, perfect phase-consistency between SOURCE and TOKENS views. Do NOT vendor Prism/highlight.js — they solve a problem you already solved in Rust.

Vendor exactly ONE third-party file: d3.v7.min.js 7.9.0 (~280 KB) pinned and committed under web/vendor/, loaded via local <script src="/vendor/d3.v7.min.js">. Use d3.tree() for the AST and d3 selections for CFG rendering. Never reference a CDN at runtime — demo machines may have no internet.

Strongest architecture for a compiler course: compute BOTH layouts server-side in Rust (tidy-tree for AST ~60 lines; longest-path layering + within-layer barycenter ordering for the CFG ~120 lines) and emit x/y/w/h in the JSON artifact. The browser becomes a pure SVG painter with zero layout code, the layout algorithms count as compiler-project work, and nothing can break offline.

If you'd rather not write CFG layout in Rust, add @dagrejs/dagre 3.1.1 dist/dagre.min.js (~100 KB, MIT) as a second vendored file — it handles back-edge routing and rank assignment far better than a quick hand-rolled pass. Avoid elkjs (1-2 MB, EPL/GPL license).

Hand-roll the benchmark bars as SVG: <rect> per measurement, y-axis ticks every nice number, value labels, hover tooltip via a positioned div, and CSS transition on height/width for animated growth — roughly 60 lines total. Chart.js UMD works offline but buys you nothing for 2 bar charts while costing 200 KB and fighting your dark theme.

Pipeline view (SOURCE->TOKENS->AST->CFG->SSA->LOOP ANALYSIS->BENCH): a horizontal stepper of chips, each phase a lazy-rendered panel, left/right arrow keys + click navigation, 150 ms opacity/translateY transition on swap. Animate SSA construction by diffing instruction ids between phases and flashing new ones; animate LICM by transitioning hoisted instructions' positions. All pure CSS + ~40 lines of JS — maximum wow, minimum fragility.

Loop-analysis verdict display: green solid-border badge + 'PARALLELIZED x N threads' for accepted loops; REJECTED loops get vermillion dashed border, a diagonal hazard-stripe SVG pattern overlay, and a tooltip listing the exact dependence cycle (array name + subscript pairs). Encode verdict redundantly (icon glyph + dash pattern + label) so it survives colorblind viewing and grayscale printing.

Palette (dark, tested conventions): page bg #0d1117, panel bg #161b22, borders #30363d, text #e6edf3. Block roles from lightened Okabe-Ito: entry #00C896 (green), exit #E8630A (vermillion), loop header #56B4E9 (sky blue), join #E5D75A (softened yellow), straight-line #8b949e on #21262d. Edges: fallthrough #6e7681, branch-taken #56B4E9, loop back-edge #E69F00 drawn curved with visible arrowheads. Syntax colors: One Dark Pro set listed in key_facts.

Keep a Graphviz escape hatch: emit .dot for the CFG alongside the web UI (~30 lines of code). Graders can render it themselves, and it cross-validates your own layout. Optional ratatui 0.30 TUI only for text-friendly phases (tokens table, SSA listing, reduction report, ASCII speedup bars) — treat as a bonus, budget it last.

For the demo, also inline the current program's JSON artifact into index.html at request time (or offer a 'Download standalone HTML' button that inlines it) so a double-clickable single file exists as a fallback if something goes wrong with the server on presentation day.
pitfalls: tiny_http has had no release since October 2022 — it works but is frozen; if anything HTTP-edge-case bites you on Win11 nobody is fixing it. axum's tokio dependency tree is heavy (~100+ transitive crates, longer clean builds) but that cost is paid once and it is the ecosystem default.

chart.umd.min.js is the ONLY Chart.js file that works via <script> tag; grabbing the npm main entry (ESM) fails silently-ish under file:// and even over HTTP in strict setups. Pin and commit whichever file you choose.

Do not rely on jsDelivr/unpkg at runtime 'with a local fallback' — demo-day machines with no internet will show a blank graph exactly when it matters. Vendoring is binary: commit the file or don't use the lib.
elkjs bundles the entire Java ELK via GWT (~1-2 MB) and is EPL-2.0/GPL-3.0 licensed — awkward heft and license for a college project when dagre does the same job at 100 KB MIT.

tower_http::ServeDir reads from the filesystem and cannot serve include_str!/include_bytes! content; mixing them naively causes 'works on my machine, 404 on the grader's'. Either embed everything or serve everything from disk — pick one per build profile.
include_str!/include_bytes! freeze asset content at compile time: edit app.js, forget to rebuild, demo shows stale UI. rust-embed's debug-mode disk reading eliminates exactly this trap.
Bind to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0 — a 0.0.0.0 bind triggers the Windows Firewall consent dialog mid-demo on locked-down college machines and may be silently blocked.
A fetch()-based frontend breaks if someone opens index.html via file:// (CORS/fetch restrictions); either always go through the server or inline the artifact JSON into the HTML.

ratatui Canvas renders braille dots — a 30-block CFG with back edges becomes unreadable noise, and BarChart cannot animate or do horizontal bars natively; building a credible TUI graph view is days of work for strictly worse visuals than the web UI. Don't let it eat your schedule.

Pure saturated colors (#FF0000, #00FF00, #F0E442 at full brightness) vibrate/halate on near-black backgrounds; darken/soften yellows and avoid red-vs-green as the ONLY distinction for parallelization verdicts (~8% of male viewers see them as identical).

SVG text measurement differs per font — if you size basic-block boxes from character counts, use a monospace stack (ui-monospace, Consolas) and pad generously, or measure with getComputedTextLength() after insertion; otherwise labels clip on Win11's default fonts.
d3 v7 UMD is safe today, but watch for v8/v9 pressure toward ESM-only: pin the vendored file to 7.9.0 and never 'refresh' it casually — it is a committed binary asset, not a dependency.
references: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/chart.js+offline (ESM main entry fails via script tag; UMD required)
Wong, B. 'Points of view: Color blindness', Nature Methods 8:441 (2011) (canonical Okabe-Ito citation)

result.summary: A defensible college-report methodology for HELIX Lite is a small hand-rolled interleaved-round harness using std::time::Instant (QPC-backed on Windows, 10 MHz / 100 ns tick), with 3+ untimed warmup rounds that absorb JIT first-call compilation (reported separately), adaptive repetition to make each sample 100-250 ms, median-of-15-plus-CV reporting, and A-B-C interleaving of interpreter/native-sequential/native-parallel to defeat thermal drift. Criterion (0.7.x) can drive FFI calls via iter_custom but its nanosecond-scale statistical machinery and per-benchmark reports are a poor fit for producing cross-variant speedup tables, so it should be at most a dev-dependency sanity check. Cheats are prevented by calling the JITed kernel through a raw function pointer, consuming results via a printed checksum shared by all three execution modes, pre-allocating/touching buffers once, padding per-thread reduction accumulators to 64-byte cache lines, and choosing (and disclosing) a cache regime. Presentation should pair a speedup table with a parallel-efficiency column, an Amdahl serial-fraction note, a self-measured STREAM-triad bandwidth ceiling for memory-bound kernels, absolute ns/elem numbers, and a hand-written-Rust anchor run so 100x+ interpreter gaps read as expected (literature range for tree-walkers on numeric loops: ~10-150x) rather than bogus.
key_facts: Rust std::time::Instant on Windows is implemented over QueryPerformanceCounter (per official docs); QPC frequency on Windows 11 is typically 10,000,000 Hz => 100 ns per tick, monotonic, fixed at boot; Instant::now() call overhead is roughly 20-30 ns, so any timed region >= 1 ms makes timer resolution and overhead negligible (<0.01%).

quanta crate latest is 0.12.3 (crates.io): RDTSC-based Clock calibrated against QPC, with Upkeep background-recalibration thread; has a known long-run drift issue (metrics-rs/quanta #91). Only worth adding for sub-microsecond regions, which HELIX kernel benchmarks are not.

Criterion latest line is 0.7.x (0.7.0 mid-2025, maintenance mode, MSRV 1.80+). Bencher::iter_custom lets you wrap FFI/JIT-pointer calls with your own clock, and std::hint::black_box (stable since Rust 1.66, best-effort identity-with-pessimism) prevents constant-folding of inputs; but criterion's output (bootstrap CIs per single benchmark, Tukey outlier classes, HTML plots) does not yield the interpreter-vs-native comparison tables the report needs.

Kalibera & Jones, 'Rigorous Benchmarking in Reasonable Time' (ISMM 2013) is the standard citation: discard warmup, ~30 repetitions gives tight confidence intervals, prefer Level-3 designs (multiple process invocations) when JIT/GC state matters, report CIs of ratios/differences rather than eyeballing overlapping intervals.

Windows noise controls: SetPriorityClass(HIGH_PRIORITY_CLASS or safer ABOVE_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS) via windows-sys; High Performance power plan (powercfg /setactive SCHEME_MIN) prevents core parking/frequency-scaling artifacts; timeBeginPeriod became per-process in Windows 10 2004, so other processes' timer requests still perturb scheduling; Sleep(1) granularity is ~15.6 ms by default.

False sharing: pad per-thread accumulators to one 64-byte cache line ([repr(align(64))] wrapper) and give each thread a contiguous block chunk, not a stride-N slice; unpadded adjacent counters can scale negatively with thread count (Preshing; TU Delft concurrency notes).

Bandwidth ceilings: dual-channel DDR5 desktops reach ~65-80 GB/s in STREAM Triad vs ~76.8-96 GB/s theoretical (70-85% rule); single-thread streams often only 20-35 GB/s, so multi-core memory-bound speedup saturates well below core count. Measure achievable BW with your own triad-shaped HELIX/Rust kernel instead of quoting the spec sheet.

Arithmetic intensities (Williams-Waterman-Patterson roofline): saxpy f64 moves 24 B/elem for 2 FLOP (AI ~0.08-0.11), scale 16 B/elem, dot product 16 B/elem for 2 FLOP (AI ~0.125) - all deeply DRAM-bound; naive matmul is low-AI until blocked, and i-k-j ordering beats naive i-j-k by ~3-5x from stride-1 access alone.

Distance-1 recurrence x[i] = a*x[i-1] + b is a first-order linear recurrence with a distance-1 flow dependence through the array (GCD test: gcd(1,1)=1 divides everything); it is NOT a reduction because intermediate stored values are needed, so auto-parallelizers must reject it - the canonical negative test for HELIX's dependence analysis.

Tree-walking interpreters on numeric loops are commonly 10-150x slower than compiled code (community consensus; Crafting Interpreters shows jlox ~an order of magnitude slower than clox alone), so a 100x+ HELIX interpreter-to-native gap is within published expectations provided per-op absolute numbers and a Rust-reference anchor are shown.

Environment capture: sysinfo 0.37.x gives CPU brand/clocks, total RAM, OS name/version/kernel programmatically in-process; hyperfine's JSON schema (command, mean/stddev/median/min/max plus full raw 'times' array) is a good model for HELIX result files; charts are best generated offline from saved JSON via a small Python/matplotlib script.

Cranelift JIT hygiene: cranelift-jit's own jit-minimal example establishes the pattern - obtain get_finalized_function pointer, transmute, call, assert/consume the result; enable set_disasm(true) (+ capstone) to inspect emitted code and prove loads/stores were not elided.

Parallel FP reductions change summation order, so parallel results cannot be bit-compared to sequential ones; min/max reductions are order-independent and bit-exact, and integer accumulation is exact - use these for strict checksum validation and relative-tolerance checks (e.g., |diff| <= 1e-9*|sum|) for FP sums.
recommendations: Build a hand-rolled ~150-line bench harness as examples/bench.rs instead of adopting criterion as the primary tool: it interleaves variants, adapts rep counts, writes JSON, and prints the report tables directly. Keep criterion 0.7 (dev-dependency, iter_custom + std::hint::black_box) only as an optional micro-region sanity check if desired.

Harness protocol per (kernel, N, variant): (1) untimed warmup round 1 triggers JIT compile - time the compile separately and report it as its own column; (2) two more untimed warmup rounds stabilize caches/branch predictors/page tables; (3) take k=15 samples, each timing R inner reps chosen so the sample lasts 100-250 ms (pick R from a pilot run per variant - the interpreter needs far fewer reps than native); (4) report median, min, and CV = stddev/mean, and rerun automatically if CV > 5%.

Interleave variants round-robin (interp, native-seq, native-par, interp, ...) rather than finishing one variant before starting the next; this defeats thermal drift and background-load drift. Fix the round order or randomize within rounds, and record which.

Run the whole suite under: HIGH (or ABOVE_NORMAL) priority via SetPriorityClass from windows-sys, High Performance power plan, AC power, Defender exclusions for the target dir, no browser open; pin nothing by default but optionally add a --pin mode using SetThreadAffinityMask and disclose it in the report.

Anti-cheat checklist baked into the harness: call the JITed kernel through a raw extern fn pointer (LLVM cannot hoist/DCE it); after timing, checksum every output array (sum of bits or FNV-1a) and print it; require all three execution modes to produce matching checksums (bit-exact for int/min/max kernels, tolerance-based for FP reductions); pre-allocate and touch all buffers once before any timing; keep data magnitudes in ~1..100 to avoid denormal penalties.

Pre-spawn the HELIX thread pool once at startup and barrier-sync each rep; include the barrier inside the timed region (honest) and additionally report a pure-compute number for one large kernel where sync cost is <1%, so readers can separate pool overhead from scaling limits. Pad per-thread reduction partials to 64 bytes and chunk iterations as contiguous blocks.

Choose the cache regime explicitly per kernel: medium sizes (N=2^20 f64, ~8-16 MB working sets) sit near LLC for steady-state runs, and large sizes (N=2^24-2^26, hundreds of MB) force DRM-bound behavior; state array footprint vs LLC size in every table caption. Skip user-space cache flushing (clflush games) - undocumented and unnecessary at these sizes.

Add a self-measured bandwidth ceiling: implement a STREAM-triad-equivalent kernel in HELIX (a[i]=b[i]+s*c[i]) plus the same in plain Rust, derive achievable GB/s, then report HELIX parallel saxpy/dot GB/s as % of that ceiling next to the speedup column - this converts 'we got 22x' into 'we reach 82% of the machine's usable bandwidth'.

Report format per kernel: columns = kernel, N, variant, median time, ns/elem, speedup vs interpreter, speedup vs native-seq, parallel efficiency E_p=S_p/p, ideal speedup p, CV%. Sweep p in {1,2,4,8,16,24,32}. Follow Hoefler-style rules: state the baseline explicitly, always show absolute performance alongside speedups, avoid log-log axes that hide inefficiency.

Frame the interpreter gap credibly: (a) lead with ns/elem per variant; (b) cite the 10-150x tree-walker range (Crafting Interpreters jlox/clox, community measurements); (c) include a hand-written Rust release-build twin of each kernel and show HELIX-native lands within ~1.2-2x of it, which validates the Cranelift pipeline and makes the 100x+ ratio arithmetically inevitable; (d) separate kernel-only from end-to-end (parse+compile+run) timings and label which is shown.

Amdahl note in the report: S_max = 1/f_serial; estimate each kernel's serial fraction (JIT dispatch, final combine, barriers) from the p=1 vs asymptotic times and show the fitted Amdahl curve overlaid on measured points; expect efficiency to drop past the physical-core count since 32 logical CPUs likely means 16 cores + SMT - present efficiency against both counts.

Reproducibility bundle: meta JSON written once per campaign (CPU brand/cores via sysinfo 0.37, total RAM, OS build, rustc --version --verbose string, cranelift/wasmtime versions from Cargo.lock, power plan, date, RNG seed, git rev); one results JSON per run modeled on hyperfine's schema including the raw per-sample times array so medians can be recomputed offline; deterministic seeded input generators shared by all variants; commit all JSONs to the repo.

Generate figures offline from saved JSON with a short Python matplotlib script (speedup-vs-threads lines per kernel, efficiency curves, roofline overlay with the measured triad ceiling, box/violin of sample distributions); save SVG or 300-dpi PNG. Keeping plotting out of the Rust binary keeps the harness dependency-free (serde_json is the only extra runtime dep).

Kernel suite with sizes tuned for a 16C/32T desktop: saxpy y+=a*x (f64, N=2^16 and N=2^24); scale y=s*x (N=2^24); dot-product reduction + (i64 accumulator option for exactness, f64 for realism; N=2^26); min/max reduction (N=2^26, bit-exact validation); distance-1 recurrence x[i]=a*x[i-1]+b (N=2^24, must be REJECTED - log the dependence-analysis verdict and run sequential); 5-point Jacobi stencil + 2D init on 4096x4096 f64 interior (134 MB/array, DRAM-bound, rows independent); matmul C=A*B at 512x512 and 768x768 f64 with outer i-loop parallel and innermost k as a recognized +-reduction (ikj ordering optional).

Include deliberate negative/small cases in the demo: N=2^12-2^16 parallel runs where threading does not pay (efficiency < 1) presented honestly, and the rejected recurrence - examiners reward a compiler that refuses unsound parallelizations and authors who admit overhead regimes.
pitfalls: FP reduction parallelization reorders additions, so parallel checksums will not match sequential ones bit-for-bit; validating with == will fail spuriously. Use min/max or integer kernels for strict equality and relative tolerance for FP sums, and document the reassociation.

The first call to a freshly compiled HELIX function includes Cranelift codegen; folding it into steady-state timings corrupts small-N numbers. Time compilation separately and exclude it from kernel samples (warmup absorbs it).
32 logical CPUs are probably 16 physical cores + SMT: expecting linear speedup to 32 invites a bogus-looking efficiency collapse around p>16. Present efficiency vs both logical and physical counts.

Windows Balanced power plan parks cores and varies boost clocks, producing multimodal timings that no amount of averaging fixes; likewise another process raising/lowering timer resolution changes scheduler churn (pre-Win10-2004 globally, per-process now). Control power plan and background state, and interleave variants so drift hits all variants equally.

Instant/QPC granularity is ~100 ns and Instant::now() costs tens of ns - harmless at >=1 ms regions but fatal if you try to time single sub-microsecond interpreter ops without batching many reps inside one timed region.

std::hint::black_box is best-effort and constant-folds expressions placed inside it (black_box(5*10) folds to black_box(50)); it protects host-side values, not the JITed body. The real protections are the raw fn-pointer call plus result checksumming - and remember HELIX's own DCE pass can delete stores of unused outputs, so the checksummed variable must be live in the HELIX source too.

Strided (round-robin) iteration assignment plus unpadded per-thread accumulators causes false sharing that can make parallel runs slower than serial; contiguous chunks and 64-byte-aligned accumulator padding are mandatory.
Denormal or huge-magnitude data can trigger 10-100x FP slowdowns on some paths and differ between interpreter and native arithmetic; initialize inputs to normal-range values.

Do not quote DDR spec-sheet bandwidth as the ceiling - desktops realize only ~70-85% of it in Triad, and single-threaded streams reach a fraction of the all-core figure; using spec-sheet numbers makes memory-bound speedup caps look like implementation failures.

Naive i-j-k matmul will be 10-100x below OpenBLAS; if included, scope the claim as 'HELIX vs its own interpreter/native modes', never vs vendor BLAS, or reviewers will flag the comparison as strawman.
Running all reps of one variant before another lets thermal/background drift bias whichever variant ran last; fixed-order blocking of variants is the most common student-methodology attack surface.
Log-log speedup plots hide severe inefficiency (Moreland/Oldfield); always tabulate efficiency numerically and keep axes linear where possible.
Adaptive rep-count differences between variants change how fixed overheads amortize; pick reps from a pilot run per variant and freeze them in the results metadata so the choice is auditable.
quanta's TSC calibration drifts from wall-clock over long sessions (issue #91) - irrelevant for short campaigns but another reason to just use Instant for millisecond-scale kernels.

Criterion's baseline-change detection assumes same-process reruns; using it across interpreter/native variants in one process conflates allocator/cache state, and its saved baselines live under target/ which gets cleaned - another reason it should not carry the report's headline numbers.

result.summary: For HELIX Lite, compute dominators with the Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy iterative immediate-dominator algorithm (roughly 80 lines, near-linear in practice) rather than Lengauer-Tarjan, derive dominance frontiers directly from the idom array, and build semi-pruned SSA by placing phis at the iterated dominance frontier of "global" variables (those with upward-exposed uses), renamed via a dominator-tree preorder walk. Keep SSA strictly scalar and leave [T] arrays as explicit load/store operations - this is the standard LLVM/GCC/Cytron precedent and is exactly what affine-subscript dependence analysis wants. Do not implement classical out-of-SSA translation at all: Cranelift IR is SSA with block parameters that are semantically phis whose arguments each predecessor terminator passes explicitly, so HELIX phis lower 1:1 to block params and the lost-copy/swap problems become regalloc2's move-coalescing job. Current crates are cranelift-codegen/-frontend/-jit 0.135.0 (published 2026-08-20, with concurrent maintenance lines 0.134.x/0.133.x/etc., so pin exact versions).
key_facts: Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy ('A Simple, Fast Dominance Algorithm', Rice): compute postorder via DFS from entry, process blocks in REVERSE postorder; idom[entry]=entry (self-sentinel), all others UNDEFINED; repeat until no change: for each b in RPO (skip entry), take first pred with idom set as new_idom, then for every other processed pred p: new_idom <- intersect(p, new_idom); write back if changed.

CHK intersect(b1,b2): two fingers start at b1,b2; while fingers differ, whichever has the SMALLER postorder number is replaced by its idom (higher postorder number = closer to root); returns the meeting node. Empirically near-linear, slightly superlinear worst case; the paper shows it competitive with tuned Lengauer-Tarjan while being dramatically simpler.

Verdict for a small project: CHK fits. Lengauer-Tarjan variants (semi-NCA/hybrid) matter for LLVM/GCC because real-world CFGs reach tens of thousands of blocks; for course-scale functions CHK is faster to write, easy to verify, and its idom array directly feeds DF computation, dominator-tree walks, and dominance queries used by CSE/LICM/verification.

Dominance frontiers from idoms, runner form (simplest, needs only the idom array): for every join b with >=2 predecessors, for each pred p: runner=p; while runner != idom[b]: { DF[runner].insert(b); runner = idom[runner]; }

Equivalent Cytron bottom-up form (TOPLAS 1991): DF(X) = DFlocal(X) UNION union over children Z of DFup(Z), where DFlocal(X)={Y in succ(X) : idom(Y)!=X} and DFup(Z)={Y in DF(Z) : idom(Y)!=X}; traverse the dominator tree children-first. Worst case O(E+N^2), usually linear because DF sets are small.

SSA flavor taxonomy: MINIMAL = phis at iterated DF of every def site, no liveness; SEMI-PRUNED (Briggs, Cooper, Harvey, Simpson, SP&E 28(8), 1998) = restrict phi insertion to 'global' names found by one linear pass computing per-block local-def sets and upward-exposed uses (UEVar); PRUNED (Choi, Cytron, Ferrante 1991) = additionally require the variable be live-in at the join, which costs a full block-level backward liveness fixpoint (UEVar/Kill per block, iterate to fixpoint).

Briggs et al.'s measurements: semi-pruned yields phi counts close to pruned at a fraction of the cost - it is the accepted sweet spot for hand-written compilers; pruned machinery (full liveness) buys little unless dead phis measurably slow later passes.

Renaming step (all flavors): preorder walk of the dominator tree carrying per-variable stacks of current SSA names; push on defs and phis, pop on exit, fill phi arguments when visiting successors (or afterwards by scanning each pred). Parameters and zero-initialized globals must be seeded as entry-block definitions so every use has a reaching def.

Alternative construction style: Braun, Buchwald, Hack, Leissa, Mallon, Zwinkau, 'Simple and Efficient Construction of Static Single Assignment Form' (CC 2013, arXiv:1211.3688) builds PRUNED SSA on-the-fly during AST->IR translation using readVariable/writeVariable, sealed/unsealed blocks for forward refs and back edges, and lazy phi creation with trivial-phi elimination. This is what cranelift-frontend's FunctionBuilder implements (its docs cite Braun et al.); relevant only if you generated straight to CLIF, which conflicts with running your own optimizer on your own IR.

Out-of-SSA destruction theory: naive phi-to-copy rewriting hits (a) the LOST-COPY problem - a value whose live range a phi split dies at the inserted copy but is still needed along another path (typically loops), and (b) the SWAP problem - parallel copies forming cycles (a,b <- b,a) produce wrong results if executed sequentially without temporaries. Canonical treatments: Sreedhar, Ju, Gillies, Santhanam (SAS'99, LNCS 1694 pp.194-210); Budimlic, Cooper, Harvey, Kennedy, Mergen, Reeves, Tian (CGO 2005); Briggs et al. 1998 section 4; textbook treatment in Rastello & Bouchez Tichadou, 'SSA-Based Compiler Design'. All require interference graphs or parallel-copy sequentialization with temp-based cycle breaking - significant machinery.

Cranelift block params: basic blocks carry parameters that ARE phis semantically; the value is selected by which incoming edge was taken. Invariant enforced by Cranelift's verifier: every terminator targeting block B (jump, brif arm, br_table arm) must pass EXACTLY len(params(B)) arguments, type-matched positionally; different predecessors may pass different values but never different arity/types. brif carries two independent argument lists (then-target and else-target).

Consequence: you can skip destruction entirely. For each HELIX block with k phis: create the CLIF block and issue k append_block_param calls in a fixed order; every predecessor terminator supplies its k values aligned to that order. regalloc2 merges the liveranges on either side of a block parameter into one bundle / coalesces the moves (Chris Fallin's regalloc2 write-up, 2022), so swap cycles and lost copies are resolved inside Cranelift's allocator, not in your code.

Scalar-only SSA precedent: Cytron et al. 1991 defines SSA over scalars; LLVM keeps register values in SSA while memory is deliberately outside SSA - mem2reg promotes only scalar allocas whose sole uses are load/store (default threshold 64 bytes), arrays indexed via GEP are never promoted, and SROA splits only aggregates with statically identifiable elements; GCC's GIMPLE uses the same model (scalar SSA + explicit memory ops). Keeping [T] accesses as load/store ops with SSA scalars is therefore mainstream and defensible, and it lets affine-subscript dependence analysis read address arithmetic directly instead of reasoning about heap SSA.

Versions verified August 2026: cranelift-codegen, cranelift-frontend, cranelift-jit 0.135.0 published 2026-08-20, alongside simultaneous maintenance releases 0.134.4, 0.133.3, 0.123.14, 0.111.13 (wasmtime ships multiple support branches concurrently); docs.rs currently documents cranelift-frontend 0.134.x with API create_block(), append_block_param(), ins.jump(blk, &[args]), brif(c, blk_t, &[], blk_f, &[]), seal_block/seal_all_blocks, finalize().
recommendations: Implement CHK iterative idoms: iterative (explicit-stack) DFS for postorder to avoid recursion-depth crashes on deep chains, process in reverse postorder, iterate to fixpoint, intersect() via postorder-number finger walk. Reuse the resulting idom tree everywhere (CSE scoping, LICM safety checks, SSA verification) - one 80-line module pays for itself across the whole optimizer.

Derive DFs with the runner-walk rule (only needs the idom array), then build SEMI-PRUNED SSA: pass 1 collects per-block local-def sets and upward-exposed uses to classify global names; for each global name run the iterated-DF worklist over its def blocks (seeding def blocks with parameters/globals from the entry block); rename with a dominator-tree preorder walk and per-variable name stacks, filling phi args from each predecessor's current mapping.

Skip pruned SSA initially. Full block-level liveness is extra code and another fixpoint to maintain; add it only if profiling shows dead phis hurting later passes. Note in the project write-up that Braun et al. 2013 gives pruned SSA for free during AST-directed construction - good related-work material even though it does not fit an optimize-existing-CFG pipeline.

Keep SSA scalar-only: i32/i64/f32/f64/bool live in SSA values; arrays stay as explicit load/store/address ops (LLVM-style). Mark loads/stores as side-effecting for CSE/DCE by default; only the affine dependence analysis may reorder/parallelize them, and only after proving independence or recognizing a supported reduction (+,-,*,min,max).

Never translate out of SSA. Lower HELIX phis mechanically to Cranelift block params: one param per phi in a deterministic order recorded in a (block -> param order) table; every predecessor terminator reads that table to build its argument list. This deletes lost-copy handling, swap-cycle breaking, parallel-copy sequentialization, and edge-split-for-copies from your scope; Cranelift + regalloc2 own those problems.

Pin exact crate versions in Cargo.toml, e.g. cranelift-codegen/cranelift-frontend/cranelift-jit = "=0.135.0". Wasmtime publishes several maintenance lines on the same day, so caret ranges can silently resolve across divergent minors; exact pins keep the documented append_block_param/jump-args API stable.

Ship a debug-mode SSA verifier invoked after EVERY pass: (a) each use is dominated by its def (def block dominates use block; intra-block ordering respected); (b) every phi has exactly one argument per predecessor, mapped 1:1, types matching; (c) no use without a reaching def. Pair it with a differential tester: run optimized JIT output against the tree-walking interpreter on randomly generated programs - this catches optimizer bugs the static checker cannot.

Centralize all CFG mutation (block deletion, edge removal, unreachable-code cleanup) behind helpers that atomically update successor phis (drop the deleted pred's argument) and mark dominator info dirty. Recompute reachability and dominators after any CFG change before running any dominance-dependent pass.
pitfalls: Unreachable blocks corrupt everything downstream: CHK and iterated-DF phi placement assume a reachable-only flowgraph; an unreachable predecessor contributes bogus phi arguments. Strip unreachable blocks (forward reachability from entry) BEFORE dominator computation and again after every CFG-mutating pass.

Infinite loops / self-loops break naive postorder DFS: exit-less regions are unreachable from exits and blocks may never be visited; decide policy up front (reject or keep) and make the DFS mark unvisited nodes unreachable rather than dereferencing UNDEFINED idoms.
Entry-block sentinel: idom(entry) = entry itself; guard intersect() and DF walkers so they stop at the entry (entry has the largest postorder number) instead of looping or indexing out of range.

Uninitialized variables: renaming fabricates uses with no reaching def. Choose semantics (zero-initialize like cranelift-frontend's silent emit_zero, or diagnose as an error) and materialize an explicit init/undef value in the entry block so phis and the verifier stay well-formed.

Critical edges: classic phi-based SSA does not need edge splitting for PLACEMENT (phis are per-block), and block params naturally carry per-edge values; but you WILL need splitting if you ever insert code that must execute on exactly one edge (instrumentation, reduction epilogues, out-of-SSA copies). Splitting after phi insertion desynchronizes phi argument lists unless the args are migrated to the new intermediate block - either split before SSA construction or update phis atomically with the split.

The most common corruption bug: deleting an edge or block without deleting the matching phi argument (or adding a pred without adding an argument). One-sided updates survive until the next dominator query or Cranelift verification, making root-causing painful; route every CFG edit through one helper.

Loop-header phis interact badly with LICM: a header phi whose backedge operand differs from its entry operand encodes the loop-carried value and must never be hoisted, nor may its inputs move above the loop unsafely. Gate LICM on 'all operands defined outside the loop' and treat non-trivial header phis as immovable.

If anyone talks you into classical destruction anyway, budget for lost-copy (phi-split live ranges dying at inserted copies, classically in loops) and swap (parallel-copy cycles needing temporaries) - Sreedhar et al. SAS'99 / Budimlic et al. CGO'05 show this is a research-grade detour. This is precisely why phi-to-block-param lowering is recommended instead.

Cranelift argument-list discipline: adding/removing a block param without updating EVERY predecessor's jump/brif argument list fails late in Cranelift's verifier ('branch passes N arguments, destination expects M'). Generate both sides from a single table to prevent skew, and remember brif needs TWO independently correct argument lists.

Optimization boundary: once IR is lowered to CLIF you cannot run YOUR passes anymore - Cranelift applies only its own built-in optimizations (opt-level settings). Keep HELIX IR as the sole optimization substrate and treat lowering as one-way and last.
