result.summary: As of August 2026 the active cranelift crate series is 0.135.0 (published 2026-08-20 alongside the latest wasmtime train), with 0.133.x/0.134.x still receiving patches and several older parallel lines (0.111.x, 0.123.x) maintained for older wasmtime LTS branches; all cranelift-* crates must be pinned to the same minor. The canonical JIT flow for the current version is: settings::builder -> cranelift_native::builder().finish(flags) -> JITBuilder::with_isa(isa, default_libcall_names()) -> JITModule::new(builder) -> declare_function/define_function -> finalize_definitions() (now returns ModuleResult<()>, the old FinalizedDefinitions guard is gone) -> get_finalized_function(FuncId) -> transmute to extern "C" fn. On Windows x64 use CallConv::WindowsFastcall (= CallConv::triple_default for the windows triple; matches Rust extern "C"), which cranelift-jit handles correctly including shadow space and RtlAddFunctionTable unwind registration. Two recent API breaks matter for HELIX Lite: MemFlags was redesigned (~wasmtime 36, early 2026) from bitflags into a handle over MemFlagsData with builder methods (notrap()/aligned()/readonly()/trusted()), and JITModule::hotswap/set_definition was removed entirely (v25 cycle), so never rely on hot-patching.
key_facts: Current versions (crates.io API, checked 2026-08): cranelift-jit and cranelift-object max_version 0.135.0 (published 2026-08-20); actively patched lines 0.134.4/0.134.3, 0.133.3, 0.123.14, 0.111.13. docs.rs 'latest' currently resolves to 0.134.3 for cranelift-jit/module/object/codegen/frontend/native. Pin ALL cranelift-* crates (cranelift, cranelift-codegen, cranelift-frontend, cranelift-module, cranelift-jit, cranelift-native, cranelift-object) to one identical minor — they share ir::* types.

Canonical minimal JIT example (verified against bytecodealliance/wasmtime main, cranelift/jit/examples/jit-minimal.rs): set flags use_colocated_libcalls=false and is_pic=false (FIXME says keep false until x64 supports it); isa_builder = cranelift_native::builder().unwrap_or_else(...); isa = isa_builder.finish(settings::Flags::new(flag_builder)); let mut module = JITModule::new(JITBuilder::with_isa(isa, cranelift_module::default_libcall_names())); signatures via module.make_signature(); declare_function(name, Linkage::Local, &sig); build bodies with FunctionBuilder/FunctionBuilderContext, bcx.finalize(module.target_config()); module.define_function(id, &mut ctx); module.clear_context(&mut ctx); module.finalize_definitions().unwrap(); let code = module.get_finalized_function(id); unsafe { mem::transmute::<_, extern "C" fn() -> u32>(code) }().

API changes to know: JITModule::finalize_definitions now has signature pub fn finalize_definitions(&mut self) -> ModuleResult<()> — older tutorials showing a returned FinalizedDefinitions lifetime-guard are outdated. JITBuilder constructors: new(libcall_names: Box<dyn Fn(LibCall)->String + Send + Sync>) -> ModuleResult<Self>, with_flags(flags: &[(&str,&str)], libcall_names), with_isa(isa: OwnedTargetIsa, libcall_names) -> Self. cranelift_native::new_host_isa() is gone; current functions are builder() / builder_with_options() / infer_native_flags() returning an IsaBuilder you .finish(flags) yourself.

Host symbol exposure: JITBuilder::symbol<K: Into<String>>(&mut self, name, ptr: *const u8) -> &mut Self, symbols(iter) for batches (later definitions override earlier), and symbol_lookup_fn(Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> Option<*const u8> + Send>) for dynamic resolution with platform fallback when the internal table misses. There is no SymbolLookupFn type on the current JITBuilder page (older releases had type SymbolLookupFn = Arc<dyn Fn(&str) -> Option<*const u8> + Send + Sync>); the callback shape is Fn(&str) -> Option<*const u8>. Resolution model: FuncId = a function (declare_function(..., Linkage::Import, &sig) creates a named import that resolves via the symbol table at finalize; declare_anonymous_function exists too); DataId = data objects (declare_data(name, linkage, writable, tls), define_data(DataId, &DataDescription)) — use DataId for read-only constant pools/literals, FuncId+symbol registration for host runtime functions. Cross-references: module.declare_func_in_func(func_id, &mut bcx.func) -> FuncRef for direct JIT->JIT calls; module.declare_data_in_func(data, &mut func) -> GlobalValue for globals.

Calling conventions (docs.rs cranelift-codegen 0.134.3 isa::CallConv): variants Fast, Tail, SystemV, WindowsFastcall ('Windows fastcall convention, also used for x64 and ARM'), AppleAarch64, Probestack, Winch, PreserveAll. Methods triple_default(triple: &Triple) -> Self (x86_64+Windows => WindowsFastcall, else SystemV) and for_libcall(flags, default_call_conv). On Windows x64 windows_fastcall passes first 4 int/ptr args in RCX,RDX,R8,R9 with 32-byte shadow space; Rust's extern "C" on x86_64-pc-windows-msvc is exactly this ABI, so declare all HELIX signatures with call_conv CallConv::WindowsFastcall (or triple_default) and transmute get_finalized_function results to extern "C" fn. Do NOT use SystemV signatures on Windows — mismatched register assignment (>4 args go to rdi/rsi/...) is silent corruption. cranelift-jit itself handles the convention correctly (wasmtime ships it on Windows); libcalls get for_libcall convention automatically.

Memory ops (InstBuilder, 0.134.3): fn load<T1: Into<MemFlagsData>, T2: Into<Offset32>>(self, Mem: Type, MemFlags: T1, p: Value, Offset: T2) -> Value; store<T1,T2>(self, MemFlags: T1, x: Value, p: Value, Offset: T2) -> Inst. Address operand must be pointer-width integer (I64 on x64) — extend loop indices with uextend/sextend I32->I64 before address math. Scaled indexing has no dedicated CLIF instruction: compute iadd(base, imul(idx_wide, 8)) or fold constant strides into the Offset32 immediate; the x64 backend's addressing-mode matching folds shift+add into base+index*scale memory operands. CLIF text form: v1 = load.i64 notrap aligned readonly v0+16.

MemFlags redesign (breaking, landed ~wasmtime 36, Jan-Feb 2026, PR bytecodealliance/wasmtime#10842): MemFlags is no longer a bitflags u8/u16; it is documented as an opaque entity index referring to a MemFlagsData stored in a MemFlagsSet inside the DataFlowGraph. Flag semantics survive as typed accessor/builder methods on MemFlagsData (trusted(), notrap(), aligned(), readonly, endianness little/big, checked for sandboxing); migration pattern MemFlags::new().with_notrap().with_aligned() -> builder style (...notrap().aligned()). Because InstBuilder::load/store take Into<MemFlagsData>, frontend code constructs MemFlagsData values; verify exact constructor spelling against cranelift/codegen/src/ir/memflags.rs for your pinned version.

Recommended MemFlags for HELIX heap arrays: notrap + aligned for element accesses into Vec/malloc-backed storage (you control alignment; set aligned only when the access size divides the element alignment), add readonly ONLY for provably-immutable memory (enables GVN/LICM hoisting safety), leave endianness default (little), do not use trusted() unless you can prove no trapping/aliasing surprises, checked is for sandbox schemes and unnecessary here.

Loop-body callback into host parallel_for: mark the body function a normal Local function in the same JITModule with WindowsFastcall sig (e.g. param [I64 iteration_index]); register the host runtime once: builder.symbol("helix_parallel_for", helix_parallel_for as *const u8) where Rust side is extern "C" fn(start: i64, end: i64, body: extern "C" fn(i64)) (or *const u8 body if you prefer casting on the host side); declare the import with declare_function("helix_parallel_for", Linkage::Import, &sig) and call it via declare_func_in_func. Obtain the raw body address only AFTER finalize_definitions(): let body_ptr: *const u8 = module.get_finalized_function(body_id). Simplest robust pattern: skip embedding the pointer in JIT code — after finalize, drive the parallel_for call from Rust, passing body_ptr cast to the extern "C" fn type. Ordering caveats: pointers are invalid until finalize_definitions succeeds, stay valid while the JITModule lives, and become invalid after unsafe module.free_memory(); hotswap/set_definition no longer exists (removed in wasmtime v25 cycle, PR #8670), so recompilation means building a fresh JITModule.

cranelift-object status (0.134/0.135): ObjectBuilder::new<V: Into<Vec<u8>>>(isa, name, libcall_names) -> ModuleResult<Self> (no relocation-model parameter anymore), with toggles per_function_section(bool), per_data_object_section(bool), unwind_info(bool) — on Windows it emits .pdata/.xdata-style SEH info rather than DWARF .eh_frame; Mach-O eh_frame is not implemented, ELF+COFF work. ObjectModule implements Module; ObjectModule::finish() -> ObjectProduct; ObjectProduct { pub object: object::write::Object<'static>, functions/data_objects SecondaryMaps } with function_symbol(FuncId), data_symbol(DataId), and emit(self) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Error> (consumes self; write bytes with std::fs::write). The object crate is re-exported so versions stay in sync. COFF format is chosen from the ISA's target triple, so configure the isa/triple as x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.

COFF/link.exe workflow and friction: emit app.obj then link.exe /OUT:app.exe app.obj /SUBSYSTEM:CONSOLE with a CRT (libcmt.lib static, or ucrt.lib+msvcrt.lib); unresolved externals like __acrt_iob_func mean missing CRT/legacy_stdio_definitions.lib; you must supply a proper entry (mainCRTStartup calling your exported main, or /ENTRY for freestanding). No COMDAT, no debug-info emission; libcalls (memcpy/memset/ceilf32...) must resolve at link time unless you registered them yourself. lld-link (rust-lld ships with the Rust toolchain) is a drop-in linker that removes the Visual Studio Build Tools dependency. This path is viable for a HELIX 'compile to .exe' demo but is strictly more setup than the JIT path.

Windows/JIT runtime facts: x64 Windows enforces DEP always; cranelift-jit allocates code memory and flips protection (VirtualProtect PAGE_READWRITE -> PAGE_EXECUTE_READ-style transitions) — works out of the box on stock Windows 11. Arbitrary Code Guard (ACG) / strict CFG process mitigations break any JIT: if the compiler exe opts into ACG via SetProcessDisallowedMsiAndScript.../process mitigation policy or manifest, executable-page creation fails at runtime — leave them off. Unwind info on x64 Windows is mandatory for anything that unwinds or backtraces through JIT frames; cranelift emits SEH .pdata/.xdata and cranelift-jit registers it with the OS (RtlAddFunctionTable lineage, PR #4785 era fixes); historical bugs were wrong image base and unsorted/partial RUNTIME_FUNCTION entries — fixed in current lines, but keep JIT invocations panic-free (wrap the transmuted call in catch_unwind in the HOST so unwinding never crosses JIT frames; Rust panics escaping into JIT code without intact unwind info crash in ntdll!RtlUnwindEx).

Other practicalities: settings flags worth setting — opt_level=speed/none, use_colocated_libcalls=false and is_pic=false (both recommended false in the official example for x64 today); probestack/enable_heapstack not needed for a course project. Context reuse pattern: module.make_context()/clear_context() and make_signature()/clear_signature() exist precisely to recycle allocations across many small functions — relevant when you JIT dozens of loop-body kernels. BranchProtection enum and JITMemoryProvider trait (SystemMemoryProvider vs ArenaMemoryProvider) are exposed by cranelift-jit 0.134 for branch-protection-targeted hosts and bulk-reserved memory, but defaults are fine.
recommendations: Pin the whole cranelift stack to one line — cranelift = "0.135", cranelift-jit = "0.135", cranelift-object = "0.135", etc. (or the fully patched 0.134.x if a transitive dep forces it) — and never mix minors; types from cranelift-codegen::ir flow through every crate.

Copy cranelift/jit/examples/jit-minimal.rs from the wasptime repo as your skeleton: settings::builder() with use_colocated_libcalls=false + is_pic=false, cranelift_native::builder().finish(flags), JITModule::new(JITBuilder::with_isa(isa, default_libcall_names())), declare/define/finalize_definitions/get_finalized_function/transmute. Ignore blog posts showing JITBuilder::new() with no args or a FinalizedDefinitions guard — they predate the current API.

Use CallConv::WindowsFastcall explicitly for every HELIX signature (params, imports, libcalls inherit via for_libcall), and type all host-facing functions in Rust as extern "C". Never emit SystemV-convention functions on Windows.

Expose the parallel runtime with builder.symbol(...) registrations made once at JITBuilder construction (print, alloc_array, helix_parallel_for, reduction helpers), then declare_function(..., Linkage::Import, &sig) per module. Keep a single registry table mapping HELIX intrinsic name -> (symbol string, Signature) so codegen stays declarative.

For array element access: keep array base as an I64 value, widen 32-bit indices with uexpand/uextend to I64, compute iadd(base, imul(idx, elem_size)) (elem_size 4/8 for f32/i32 and f64/i64), and load with ins().load(types::F64, flags_notrap_aligned, addr, 0). Add readonly only to loads LICM proved invariant-safe.

Drive parallel_for from the HOST side: after finalize_definitions(), grab the loop-body pointer via get_finalized_function and invoke your own thread pool from Rust. This avoids embedding finalized addresses as iconst literals in JIT code and eliminates finalize-order hazards; reserve the JIT-calls-parallel_for-with-iconst-pointer pattern for the demo slide where you want the IR to look self-contained.

Wrap every host->JIT call site in std::panic::catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(...)) and treat JIT frames as no-unwind territory; verify once on your machine that a Rust backtrace captured inside a JIT frame resolves (proves unwind registration works on your Windows 11 box).

Do the standalone-.exe stretch goal with cranelift-object + rust-lld (lld-link) rather than requiring full MSVC Build Tools: ObjectBuilder::new(isa_msvc_triple, "helix", default_libcall_names()).unwind_info(true), finish()->ObjectProduct, emit()->Vec<u8>, fs::write to .obj, then link with CRT libs; budget time for CRT/entry-symbol friction and consider emitting a C-main stub instead of /ENTRY hacks.

Write a tiny smoke test early that JITs 'fn f(x: f64) -> f64 { x * 2.0 }' and compares against native eval on all 32 logical CPUs under load — it will catch calling-convention, MemFlags-API, and unwind-registration problems in minutes instead of during the parallelization milestone.

Check docs.rs for YOUR pinned version before coding against MemFlags: the bitflags->MemFlagsData refactor changed construction syntax in early 2026; confirm the exact builder methods (notrap/aligned/readonly/trusted) from the memflags.rs source of that release.
pitfalls: Stale tutorials abound: JITBuilder::new() without libcall_names, cranelift_native::new_host_isa(), finalize_definitions returning a FinalizedDefinitions guard, and hotswap/set_definition all no longer exist or changed. Anything dated before ~mid-2025 is suspect; diff against the jit-minimal.rs example on wasmtime main instead.
Mixing cranelift-* crate minors fails to compile (ir::Function/Signature type mismatches) with confusing errors — lockstep-pin everything.

Using SystemV call_conv on Windows produces code that reads args from rdi/rsi/rcx... while callers pass in rcx/rdx/r8/r9: with <=4 scalar args it may appear to WORK by luck (rcx/rdx coincide) and then corrupt silently at 5+ args or with floats mixed in. Always WindowsFastcall.

MemFlags::new().with_aligned() style code from pre-2026 examples will not compile after the MemFlags/MemFlagsData refactor (~wasmtime 36); conversely guessing the NEW builder-method names from memory risks errors — check memflags.rs for the exact pinned release.

get_finalized_function before finalize_definitions, keeping the pointer past module.free_memory(), or dropping the JITModule while worker threads still execute loop bodies = dangling executable memory. The module must outlive all in-flight parallel work.

Panics or C++-style unwinding crossing a JIT frame on Windows relies on RUNTIME_FUNCTION unwind metadata; an escape route through unregistered or mis-based code crashes deep in ntdll!RtlUnwindEx. Contain panics on the host side.

Enabling process mitigations (Arbitrary Code Guard, or strict CFG policies) for your compiler exe will make cranelift-jit fail to create executable pages at runtime — leave mitigations off for the JIT configuration; also note JIT code addresses are not valid CFG indirect-call targets if you ever compile the host with /guard:cf enforcement.
is_pic=true/use_colocated_libcalls=true are still flagged unsupported on x64 in the official example — keep them false or you get relocation failures in the JIT.

cranelift-object COFF path pitfalls: forgetting CRT libs gives unresolved __acrt_iob_func/__imp_* errors; libcalls (memcpy, fmodf, ceil) must come from somewhere; no debug info means debugger sessions show raw addresses; emit() consumes ObjectProduct so you cannot emit twice.
Load/store address operands MUST be pointer-width (I64): loading with an I32 address is a verifier error, and forgetting uextend on 32-bit loop indices is the single most common frontend bug.

readonly flag on mutable shared arrays lets the optimizer hoist loads out of loops whose iterations another thread mutates — with automatic parallelization this becomes a real data-race-as-optimizer-bug; only mark readonly for genuinely immutable data.
crates.io's 'newest_version' field (0.123.14) disagrees with 'max_version' (0.135.0) because old wasmtime-LTS lines still receive patch publishes; don't interpret 0.123.x as the current stable line.

result.summary: For HELIX Lite's helix_parallel_for(start,end,body_fn_ptr,ctx,nthreads), the best teaching-value-plus-performance design is a two-stage runtime: v0 = std::thread::scope spawn-per-call with static contiguous chunks (trivially correct, makes fork/join cost measurable), upgraded to v1 = a persistent worker pool woken per parallel region with either static equal chunks (optimal for uniform memory-bound loops) or OpenMP-guided scheduling via one relaxed atomic fetch_add counter (chunk = remaining/nthreads, min-clamped). Reductions must use per-thread partials padded to their own 128-byte cell (crossbeam CachePadded convention) combined serially after join — never atomics in the hot loop and never unpadded accumulator arrays, which measurably cost 2–10x. Honest benchmark expectations on a dual-channel DDR5 desktop: saxpy-style kernels at 50M elements are capped by ~65–85 GB/s achievable DRAM bandwidth, giving roughly 4–6x speedup at 8–16 threads (parallel efficiency 25–60%), while cache-resident compute-bound kernels scale near-linearly (12–15x at 16 threads); report achieved GB/s versus measured STREAM-triad peak rather than raw "speedup".
key_facts: std::thread::scope (stable since Rust 1.63, doc: doc.rust-lang.org/std/thread/fn.scope.html) auto-joins all spawned threads on scope exit and panics if an auto-joined thread panicked; it borrows non-'static data via the 'env lifetime. It adds ~zero overhead over raw spawn — the cost is N kernel thread creations plus one join barrier.

Thread spawn cost: Rust std::thread on Windows maps to CreateThread; measured spawn+join cycles are ~50–100 us per thread on Windows 11 versus ~20–35 us on Linux (Stack Overflow 'How expensive is it to spawn a thread in Rust', community 2024 benchmarks on Ryzen 7950X ~55–80 us). One real project measured std::thread::scope dispatch at ~0.4 ms total and switched to a warm pool; a criterion-based gist found std_thread_scope 'so abysmal for light loads it had to be removed from log-scale charts'.

Warm-pool dispatch cost is ~0.5–5 us (Win32 SubmitThreadpoolWork measurements) versus 20–300 us for CreateThread (Raymond Chen cites ~1M cycles including stack-commit page faults); break-even around 10–50 tasks. Fork/join/barrier cost for an already-assembled team is ~1–5 us per parallel region at 32 threads (Fastbar arXiv:2407.04561: pthread barrier 48 threads ~4.4 us, lock-free ~1.6 us; TaskFlow measures trivial parallel-for launch overhead ~2–10 us at 32 threads).

Intel OpenMP runtime spins by default KMP_BLOCKTIME=200 ms before sleeping workers (Intel oneAPI docs); OMP_WAIT_POLICY=ACTIVE/PASSIVE overrides; barrier arrival/departure sub-us while workers spin. This spin-then-block hybrid is the industry-standard idle policy and the model for HELIX's pool.

Guided self-scheduling (Polychronopoulos & Kuck 1987): chunk = remaining_iterations / nthreads clamped to a minimum, claimed via atomic fetch_add on a shared next-index counter; this is exactly how GCC libgomp (gomp_loop_guided_next in libgomp/loop.c: left = end - next; chunk = left / nthreads; floor to ws->chunk_size; __sync_fetch_and_add(&ws->next, chunk)) and LLVM libomp (kmp_dispatch.cpp) implement schedule(guided).

OpenMP schedule guidance (openmp.llvm.org, LLNL tutorial): static = best for uniform-cost and memory-bound loops (contiguous per-thread streams preserve hardware prefetching and page locality, zero runtime overhead); dynamic chunk=1 self-scheduling is commonly 1.5–3x slower than static on balanced loops purely from cacheline ping-pong on the counter plus broken prefetch streams; dynamic/guided with chunk 8–64 recovers 80–95% of static performance under moderate imbalance; guided beats plain dynamic by ~10–30% on irregular work.

Static partition formula (GCC libgomp iter.c, matches OpenMP spec option 2): q = n / nthreads; t = n % nthreads; thread i gets start = q*i + min(i,t), len = q + (i < t) — first t threads get one extra iteration; the spec forbids relying on the exact split.

False sharing: two threads writing distinct variables on the same 64-byte line force MESI invalidation traffic (~40–100+ cycles per transfer vs ~4 for an L1 hit). Measured magnitudes: Martin Thompson's classic Java demo ~450M ops/s unpadded vs ~1B+ padded (mechanical-sympathy.blogspot.com 2011); Preshing's increment benchmark ~1.2 ns/inc single-threaded vs ~12 ns/inc under 4-thread false sharing (~10x); Intel's 'Avoiding and Identifying False Sharing Among Threads': expected 4x speedup collapses to ~0.4–0.5x unpadded, padding restores ~3.8x; literature range 2–10x, up to 15x worst-case (Wikipedia/ACM studies).

Padding width: use 128 bytes, not 64. crossbeam_utils::CachePadded (v0.8.22, crates.io) pads to N=128 on x86-64/aarch64/powerpc64 because Intel spatial prefetchers pull pairs of 64-byte lines; Rust idiom is #[repr(align(128))] struct Cell(T). crossbeam-utils also ships Backoff (spin_loop -> yield_now -> exponential sleep to 10 ms) implementing the canonical bounded-spin idle strategy.

Reduction combine patterns: per-thread partials combined after the join beat atomics whenever update rate is high — Fedor Pikus (CppCon 2017) measured 10–50x slowdown for contended fetch_add vs thread-local accumulation; Herlihy & Shavit ch.12 formalizes combining trees (O(log P) depth) as the scalable alternative. For min/max there is no native x86 float atomic min/max, so atomics require CAS retry loops that degrade worse than fetch_add; per-thread min/max + final combine is strongly preferred. TBB parallel_reduce is built on exactly the private-accumulator + join pattern. OpenMP 5.x reduction clause: privatize per implicit task with monoid initializer (+ -> 0, * -> 1, min -> type MAX, max -> type MIN), combine at region end in an UNSPECIFIED order — the spec explicitly warns floating-point results are not bitwise-reproducible run-to-run.

Cost threshold heuristics: canonical OpenMP if-clause example is #pragma omp parallel for if(n > 10000) (LLNL tutorial); when if(false) the region executes serialized 'as if' num_threads(1) and nested regions serialize too (unlike num_threads(1)). Hager & Wellein (Introduction to HPC): each thread needs ~10^4–10^5 useful operations to amortize startup; for light vector loops break-even can be millions of iterations. Community consensus floor: >= 1000–10000 lightweight iterations per thread; compute-heavy bodies profit from tens per thread. Fork/join overhead ~1–10 us per region (U. Oregon CIS635 notes).

Bandwidth arithmetic for the demo (50M f32 elements): saxpy moves 12 B/element (read x 4 + read y 4 + write y 4) = 600 MB/pass; daxpy 24 B/el = 1.2 GB; f64 reduction reads 8 B/el = 400 MB. Dual-channel DDR5-5200 (7950X stock) achieves ~65–70 GB/s STREAM triad; DDR5-6000 tuned ~82–88 GB/s (Phoronix/TechPowerUp); dual-channel DDR4-3200 ~42–46 GB/s. So the saxpy wall-clock floor is ~0.6 GB / 70 GB/s ~= 8.6 ms regardless of thread count.

Measured saxpy scaling: single-threaded scalar saxpy reaches only ~8–12 GB/s (~30% of peak; Karl Rupp's vectorization study shows scalar ~30% vs AVX ~90%+ of peak), giving a theoretical ceiling near 6x; course/Stack Overflow reports at n=1e8 consistently show ~1.9x @2T, ~3.5x @4T, 5–6x @8T, then flat — parallel efficiency at 16 threads typically 25–40% for DRAM-streaming kernels. Cache-resident FMA-dense kernels show the contrast: 15.2–15.9x at 16 threads on the same machines (LBNL roofline materials, scicomp SE worked examples: FMA chain 15.9x vs memcpy-class 3.2x at 16T).

Roofline framing for honesty: saxpy arithmetic intensity ~1/6 FLOP/byte (Cornell Virtual Workshop) puts every modern CPU in the bandwidth-bound region; Speedup ~= min(compute-scaling, bandwidth-scaling); teaching labs (Berkeley CS267 hw1 style) grade on achieved GB/s as % of measured STREAM peak, where 50–85% is a realistic good result.

Windows/hardware specifics: std::thread::available_parallelism() on Windows respects the process affinity mask and job-object CPU-rate limits (uses GetActiveProcessorCount(ALL_PROCESSOR_GROUPS) + GetProcessAffinityMask; rust PR #97925); returns logical CPUs (32 for a 16c/32t Ryzen). hardware_concurrency() ignores affinity and is group-limited on >64-LP systems (processor groups only matter on Threadripper/Xeon-W class parts). No NUMA concerns on single-socket AM5/LGA1700 desktops — UMA, ignore first-touch tuning (ServeTheHome/Intel single-socket guidance).

Hybrid P/E cores (Intel 12th-gen+) are a real hazard for static-partitioned parallel-for: with equal chunks and a join barrier, total time = slowest E-core thread. Documented cases: llama.cpp #842 (13900K: 24 threads gave ~50% utilization; ~10 threads pinned to 8 P-cores was ~10% faster overall), llama.cpp discussion #572 (12700F: 2–3x slower with E-cores active), Intel oneMKL officially recommends P-cores-only (KMP_HW_SUBSET=1p). Windows 11 offers soft hints SetThreadSelectedCores/CPU Sets (learn.microsoft.com 'Thread Scheduling on Hybrid Architectures'); Rust std exposes no affinity API (rust-lang/rust#91009 open) — use core_affinity crate or windows-rs if desired. AMD Zen desktop has no E-cores; SMT siblings share FPU ports so physical-core-count threads often beat logical-CPU count for FP-heavy bodies.

Rust std parking on Windows is backed by WaitOnAddress/WakeByAddressSingle (library/std/src/sys/pal/windows/thread_parking.rs), i.e. futex-equivalent; condvar wake latency on Windows measured 6–30 us (alexanderhoughton.co.uk benchmarks) — hence spin-first. Lost-wakeup requires setting the sleeper flag atomically AFTER re-checking for work and unparking only if the flag was set (rayon src/sleep.rs, Mara Bos 'Rust Atomics and Locks', blog.m-ou.se/condvars).

Cranelift (latest umbrella/cranelift-jit 0.135.0, published 2026-08-20, MSRV 1.86): JITModule/Module/Context are NOT Sync — compile and finalize_definitions on one thread, but finalized function pointers are plain executable memory safe to call concurrently from all pool workers (docs.rs/cranelift-jit, bytecodealliance FAQ, issue #731). Pointers in Cranelift IR are i64 (pointer_type()); Win64 ABI passes the first four integer/pointer args in RCX,RDX,R8,R9 with mandatory caller-allocated 32-byte shadow space (Cranelift call conv windows_fastcall handles this in abi_impl.rs) — so a host fn helix_parallel_for(i64 start, i64 end, i64 body_fn_ptr, i64 ctx, i64 nthreads) declared with pointer_type()/i64 params links cleanly against JIT'd callers.

Work-stealing deques (Chase-Lev, Le et al. PPoPP'13) are overkill for a flat parallel_for: the Apache Arrow 'Work Stealing Thread Pool Investigation' concluded a simple mutex/counter design matched Chase-Lev macro-benefits on non-NUMA hardware ('not worth it'; complexity forces raw pointers and TSAN false positives). Pedagogical ladder: global atomic counter -> per-worker deques -> lock-free Chase-Lev.
recommendations: Ship both runtimes and benchmark them against each other as a course exercise: Stage A = std::thread::scope(|s| ...) spawning nthreads-1 workers per call with static chunks (~100 LOC, zero unsafe beyond the raw body-fn-pointer call); Stage B = persistent pool (Vec of workers created once, Condvar-or-park based, bounded spin of a few hundred spin_loop() iterations then park). Students then measure the fixed overhead delta (~100 us -> ~2 us per region) — this is the single most instructive graph in the project.

Default scheduler = static contiguous equal chunks using the libgomp formula (q = n/P, t = n%P, first t threads get q+1), and ALIGN chunk boundaries to 64-byte multiples so adjacent threads never straddle a cache line in the output array. Expose schedule(static|guided|dynamic,k) as a language/runtime knob so students can reproduce the 1.5–3x dynamic-vs-static gap themselves.

Implement dynamic/guided as ONE relaxed-ordering AtomicI64 next-index fetched via compare_exchange/fetch_add with chunk = max(min_chunk, remaining/nthreads) — 15 lines, mirrors libgomp, no Chase-Lev deque. Pad the counter in its own CachePadded cell. Do not attempt per-thread deques for v1.

Reduction lowering: allocate a Vec of #[repr(align(128))] cells (or crossbeam_utils::CachePadded<T>, crossbeam-utils 0.8.22) holding per-thread accumulators initialized to the monoid identity (+/-: 0, *: 1, min: +INF/type MAX, max: -INF/type MIN); the JIT body writes its thread's slot; after join the coordinator folds slots in a trivial serial loop (O(P) <= 32 ops, unmeasurable). Never emit atomic RMW into the hot loop; reserve atomics only as a 'what not to do' demo.

Document (and test with tolerance) that float + and * reduction results are order-dependent and may differ run-to-run from the sequential baseline — quote the OpenMP spec's 'order of combination is unspecified' clause; integer reductions are exact. Make tests compare with relative epsilon or sort-free exact match only for i32/i64.

Cost-model gate mirroring OpenMP's if clause: run serial when n < max(K_MIN, GRAIN * nthreads) with GRAIN ~= 1024 for light bodies (or estimate work_us = n * per_iter_cost and require >= ~50–100 us), and cap nthreads at std::thread::available_parallelism(). Provide env override (HELIX_NTHREADS, HELIX_SCHEDULE) for scaling-study labs. Print the decision when a verbose flag is set — great for grading.

Benchmark narrative template for the report: bytes_moved = n * sizeof(T) * (loads + stores); achieved_GBps = bytes / time; plot achieved_GBps alongside speedup-vs-serial and annotate the machine's measured STREAM-triad peak. State up front: 'at 50M f32 elements saxpy moves 600 MB; our dual-channel DDR5 tops out near X GB/s, so the theoretical maximum speedup from Y GB/s single-threaded is ~Y/X — we measured Z.' Expect ~4–6x @ 8–16T for saxpy, 12–15x for cache-resident compute-bound kernels.

Pool hygiene details that will otherwise bite: (1) wake workers by flipping state BEFORE enqueueing and unpark conditionally (lost-wakeup fence); (2) workers re-check for work after being woken (spurious wakeups are legal per std::thread::park docs); (3) warm the pool with one dummy parallel region before timing — the first region pays lazy thread creation; (4) bound the idle spin (few us, crossbeam Backoff pattern) then park so serial phases aren't starved by spinning workers; (5) take median of >= 5 timed reps.

For the Cranelift side: declare helix_parallel_for with signature (pointer_type, pointer_type, pointer_type, pointer_type, pointer_type)->() or i64 params under the windows_fastcall call conv, register it as a JIT symbol; compile/finalize the module once on the main thread, then let every pool worker call the body_fn_ptr(ctx, i, end) directly — finalized JIT code is fully re-entrant. Ensure generated index arithmetic sext's i32->i64 before address computation (50M f64 = 400 MB exceeds what sloppy i32 offset math tolerates in edge cases).

Add one optional lab: detect hybrid topology (GetLogicalProcessorInformationEx EfficiencyClass via windows crate) or simply rerun with HELIX_NTHREADS = 8 vs 32 on an Intel hybrid machine, showing E-core stragglers capping speedup at the slowest thread — and optionally pin with SetThreadAffinityMask/core_affinity to demonstrate recovery.
pitfalls: Spawn-per-call on Windows is 50–100 us PER THREAD (CreateThread + CRT/TLS init + stack commit); a 16-thread parallel-for costs ~1–2 ms fixed. Any loop shorter than ~5 ms loses to the serial version. Fine for your 50M-element demos (~9 ms), fatal for small-n tests.

Naive shared accumulator: an unpadded array of f64/u64 partials (adjacent elements on one line) or one atomic add per iteration will show 2–10x and 10–50x slowdowns respectively at higher thread counts — these are the two most likely ways students 'discover' negative scaling. Both are preventable with align(128) cells + post-join fold.

Atomic counter with chunk=1 destroys memory-bound throughput twice over: cacheline ping-pong on the counter AND broken per-thread prefetch streams (each grab lands on a different core). Always clamp chunk >= 8–64, prefer remaining/P guided decay for uniform loops.

E-core straggler effect on Intel hybrid chips: static equal partitions + join means wall time = slowest E-core thread; documented 2–3x regressions versus P-core-only configs (llama.cpp #842/#572, Intel MKL guidance). AMD Zen desktop unaffected; SMT siblings contend for FPU ports so logical-CPU-count threads can underperform physical-core-count for FP bodies.

FP reduction nondeterminism: per-thread partial combine order varies run-to-run; exact-equality unit tests against the sequential result will intermittently fail for float +/*. Also '-' reduction lowers to '+ negate' with the same caveat.

Lost-wakeup races in a hand-rolled park pool: if the sleeper flag is set AFTER checking the queue, or unpark is skipped because 'it can't be sleeping yet', workers hang forever. Follow the rayon/std futex discipline (flag set after re-check; unpark only if flag was set; always re-check after waking).

Spinning forever between regions starves the main thread and other processes during serial phases (the problem KMP_BLOCKTIME exists to manage); conversely pure condvar sleep costs 6–30 us wake on Windows and can exceed the whole region for small loops. Bound the spin.
First timed parallel region includes lazy thread creation and cold TLB/pages; benchmarks will understate steady-state speedup unless the pool is pre-warmed and arrays are touched once before timing.

JITModule is !Sync: calling define_function/finalize_definitions while workers execute previously finalized code paths is fine, but compiling new functions concurrently from pool threads is not — funnel all compilation through the main thread or a mutex.

Chunk boundaries misaligned to cache lines put two threads' last/first elements on one line of the OUTPUT array — false sharing even with perfect scheduling; round chunk sizes up to 16 f32 / 8 f64 elements.

available_parallelism() can return a value shrunk by process affinity masks, job objects, Process Lasso/efficiency-mode tools, or WSL/sandbox environments — don't hard-assert it equals 32; also processor groups (>64 LPs, Threadripper PRO) can hide CPUs from older APIs.

Ignoring the memory ceiling in the write-up invites overclaiming: claiming 'near-linear 16x' for saxpy is falsifiable by any grader with a calculator (600 MB / 8.6 ms floor). Report achieved GB/s vs measured STREAM peak, and explain the plateau as bandwidth saturation, not a bug.

i32 iteration/index arithmetic in generated code: 50M fits i32, but intermediate byte offsets (i * size_of::<T>()) overflow i32 for f64 arrays past ~268M elements and generally after promotion mistakes — sext to i64 before address math.

result.summary: Classical loop-dependence analysis is layered: normalize the loop, pair up memory references on the same base array, classify each pair RAW/WAR/WAW, and run a cheap-to-expensive "battery" of tests (ZIV, Strong/Weak-Zero/Weak-Crossing SIV, then GCD-MIV and Banerjee-MIV) where any test that succeeds proves independence; anything unproven is conservatively treated as a real dependence. Each test outputs refinement of a direction vector (<,=,>,*) and occasionally an exact distance vector; the dependence LEVEL (first non-"=" component) tells which loop it blocks, and a loop is DOALL-parallelizable iff no non-reduction dependence is carried at its level. LLVM's DependenceAnalysis.cpp is a direct, readable implementation of exactly this scheme (Goff/Kennedy/Tseng PLDI'91) and, together with LLVM's DDG doc (SCC "pi-blocks" mark recurrence cycles), provides the blueprint for a minimal per-nest dependence graph and a "Loop #N: RAW n / WAR n / WAW n => SAFE" report. For HELIX Lite's tiny subscript grammar (i, i+c, c-i, c*i; 2D i,j in one perfectly nested double loop) every test becomes exact closed-form arithmetic on widened (i64/i128) integers, with reductions (x = x (+,-,*,min,max) t) exempted as the only sanctioned distance-1 self-dependence. Anti/WAR and WAW dependences are storage-reuse artifacts eliminable by renaming/privatization/scalar-and-array expansion (mention-only in the report; your SSA IR already removes scalar false dependences).
key_facts: Dependence taxonomy: flow/true (RAW) = earlier write, later read; anti (WAR) = earlier read, later write; output (WAW) = two writes; input (RAR) = two reads and NEVER blocks reordering or parallelization. Source = earlier access, sink = later access.

Distance vector d = integer iteration-count differences (sink iteration - source iteration) per nest level, e.g. for i=2..N: a[i]=a[i-1]+b[i] carries RAW a with distance <1>. Direction vector abstracts it to symbols < (d<0), = (d=0), > (d>0), * (unknown); Allen & Kennedy also use dependence level = position of leftmost non-'=' component (+1); all-'=' means loop-independent.

Core theorem (Allen & Kennedy Ch.2/Ch.4): a dependence is legal only if its distance/direction vector is lexicographically positive; loop L_k can run in parallel iff no dependence is CARRIED at level k (its first non-'=' entry is not at position k). This is the formal justification for '=> SAFE'.

GCD test (necessary condition, proves independence only): the Diophantine equation sum(c_k * i_k) = delta has an integer solution only if gcd(all coefficients) divides delta. It IGNORES loop bounds; passing it does NOT prove a dependence exists. Example: a[2*i]=a[i] -> i=2j, gcd(2,1)=1 divides 0, GCD inconclusive though dependences exist.

Banerjee test / inequalities ('Extreme Value Test', Wolfe Sec 2.5.2): for each direction, bound the subscript difference f(src)-g(dst) over the constrained iteration ranges; independence for a direction is proven iff 0 lies outside [L_min, U_max]. Necessary condition only. Worked Wikipedia example: for(i=0;i<10;i++){c[i+9]=a[i]+b[i]; d[i]=c[i]+e[i];} gives antidependence broken (1 <= -9 <= 9 fails) but true dependence not broken (-9 <= -9 <= 0 holds) => parallelizable with statements kept in order.

SIV battery (subscript-by-subscript, exact when each subscript holds <=1 index variable; from Goff/Kennedy/Tseng 'Practical Dependence Testing' PLDI'91 pp.15-29): ZIV (constants both sides: dep iff equal, direction '='); Strong SIV (a*i+p = a*i'+q: distance d=(q-p)/a if divisible else INDEPENDENT; direction from sign of d); Weak-Zero SIV (a*i+p = c: single point i*=(c-p)/a must be integral and inside [L,U]; LLVM refines to '<=' when it hits the first iteration and '>=' when it hits the last); Weak-Crossing SIV (a*i+p = -a*i'+q: crossing x=(q-p)/(2a); integral+in-bounds permits BOTH '<' and '>', odd numerator kills '=', non-integral/out-of-bounds proves independence). MIV (multiple index vars) falls back to GCD-MIV then Banerjee-MIV.

Per-dimension combination rule: results are conjoined; ONE dimension proving independence kills the whole multidimensional dependence; surviving direction vectors intersect componentwise; distance vector is known only when every component is uniquely determined.

Ordering constraints per pair: distinct statements s1-before-s2 allow (i==j, s1<s2) [loop-independent dep] OR i<j [carried]; same statement requires strict i<j. Address equality must hold in EVERY dimension simultaneously.

LLVM implementation facts (verified in llvm/lib/Analysis/DependenceAnalysis.cpp @ main, Aug 2026): header states it is an incomplete implementation of Goff/Kennedy/Tseng PLDI'91; functions strongSIVtest, weakZeroSIVtestImpl, weakCrossingSIVtest, gcdMIVtest, banerjeeMIVtest; each returns true == 'dependence disproved'; FullDependence result carries per-level DV{Distance, Direction} bitflags LT/EQ/GT; strong SIV computes Delta=sdivrem(DstStart-SrcStart, Coeff) and maps remainder!=0 to independence; Banerjee widens ALL arithmetic to WideBits = 2*BaseBits + MaxLevels + 1 bits to prevent bound-computation overflow, and uses backedge-taken counts as bounds ('a single-iteration loop has bound 0, making < and > impossible'); gcd-MIV additionally tries to disprove '=' per level (Wolfe book p.235 technique); delinearization (-da-delinearize) recovers multi-dim subscripts from flattened C arrays.

LLVM DDG structure (llvm/docs/DependenceGraphs/index.rst, verified): nodes = instructions (grouped into multi-instruction nodes), memory edges carry flow/anti/output/input deps, strongly-connected components become one-level-deep 'pi-blocks' representing recurrence cycles that block reordering; built via DependenceGraphBuilder builder-pattern (cites Kuck/Kuhn/Padua/Leasure/Wolfe POPL'81 and Ferrante/Ottenstein/Warren PDG TOPLAS'87). NOTE: the old llvm.org/docs/DependenceAnalysis.html URL currently returns 404 - the page was removed from the docs tree while DependenceAnalysis.cpp still ships; cite the source file instead.

GCC comparison point: parloops/-ftree-parallelize-loops=n performs automatic loop parallelization gated by dependence proof; the isl-based Graphite framework became default-on at -O3/-Ofast/-Os in GCC 15 (2025) and remains present in GCC 16 trunk (not removed). Polly (LLVM) does exact dependence relations via ISL for comparison in your report.

Reduction recognition rules: scalar x is a reduction iff x appears on both sides as exactly x = x op t or x = t op x with op associative (and commutative), written once per iteration, no OTHER reads/writes of x in the body, the ONLY cross-iteration dependence touching x is that self-dependence (typically distance 1); then give each thread a private accumulator seeded with the identity (+:0, *:1, min:+MAX/+inf, max:-MIN/-inf) and combine after join; copy the final value out afterward (OpenMP 'lastprivate'-like semantics). OpenMP supports reduction ops +,-,*,&,|,^,&&,||,max,min for C/C++ (max/min since OpenMP 3.1). FLOATING-POINT +/* are NOT associative (f32/f64): reassociation changes rounding - gate behind a fast-math-style flag or warn, matching what icc/gcc/clang document.

Same-statement different-subscript case: a[i]=a[i-1]+1 -> store a[i] (src) vs load a[i-1] (sink): Strong SIV gives d=(0-(-1))/1=1 => distance-1 RAW carried at level 1 => loop must stay serial (DOACROSS/hyperplane only). Contrast a[i]=b[i]+1: all deps loop-independent => DOALL-safe. Reduction contrast: s+=a[i] looks like distance-1 RAW on s but is exempt via reduction recognition.

HELIX-Lite-sized exact algorithm (all subscripts affine in one index per dim): normalize loop to i in [L,U], N=U-L+1>=1; do ALL subscript/bound arithmetic in i64 (or i128), never in the element's width; per dimension dispatch: ZIV exact; Strong SIV exact (divisibility + bounds check i, i+d in [L,U]); Weak-Zero SIV exact (integral point in range); Weak-Crossing SIV exact (crossing point); general unequal-coefficient case like a[c*i] vs a[i] (c!=1): solve a*i-b*j=k, let g=gcd(a,b); k%g!=0 => none, else parametric solutions i=i0+(b/g)t, j=j0+(a/g)t intersected with the [L,U]^2 box - empty box proves independence, nonempty yields direction '*' (optionally compute minimum positive distance by ceil/floor on t); nonlinear/unknown => assume dep '*'. Any dimension NO-DEP => no dependence; else emit (kind, level, distance-or-direction). Verdict SAFE-for-level-k iff no emitted RAW/WAR/WAW has level k after reduction exemptions.

Report shape mirroring real tools: per nest emit 'Loop #N (file:line): depth 2'; then one line per candidate pair 'a[] : S1(store)->S2(load) RAW dist=<1> dir=< > level=1'; finish with 'Loop #N: RAW 0 / WAR 0 / WAW 0 => SAFE (parallelize, k threads)' or '=> SEQUENTIAL (RAW carried at level 1)' / '=> REDUCTION (+ on s) => PARALLEL with private accumulators'.

Elimination of false dependences (mention-only material): anti(WAR)+output(WAW) come from STORAGE REUSE, not dataflow (Kuck/Padua lineage); renaming kills them for scalars - HELIX's SSA IR already eliminates scalar anti/WAW by construction, which is worth stating explicitly in the report; remaining techniques: scalar expansion (s -> s[i] array so each iteration writes its own slot), array expansion / privatization (per-thread private copy of an array or section; correctness needs first-iteration reads to see the original values and final-value propagation for last-private semantics), OpenMP private/firstprivate/lastprivate clauses as the user-directed equivalent (Allen & Kennedy Ch.3; Wolfe Ch. on eliminating dependences).

Current toolchain versions checked on crates.io (Aug 2026): cranelift, cranelift-codegen, cranelift-native, cranelift-jit all at 0.135.0; rayon 1.12.0. std::thread::scope (stable since Rust 1.63) is sufficient to fan a JIT-ed kernel out over ~32 logical CPUs by slicing the array into chunks and joining partial results; finalize_definitions() must complete before threads spawn, and calling finalized functions concurrently afterwards is supported.

Book anchors: Allen & Kennedy 'Optimizing Compilers for Modern Architectures: A Dependence-Based Approach' (Morgan Kaufmann 2001, ISBN 978-1558602861) - Ch.2 'Dependence: Theory and Practice' (vectors, levels; Sec 2.6 dependence testing incl. GCD + Banerjee, ~pp.63-81), Ch.3 Single-Loop Transformations (renaming/expansion), Ch.4 Parallel Loop Transformations (level-based parallelization algorithm), Ch.7 'Dependences Between Memory References', Ch.8 'Dependence Testing' (ZIV/SIV/MIV battery, Omega test); numbering shifts slightly between printings. Muchnick 'Advanced Compiler Design and Implementation' (1997, ISBN 978-155860320-2) - Ch.3 'Advanced Data Dependence' (starts p.61; subscript classes, GCD, Banerjee, dependence graphs) and Ch.18 'Loop Transformations' (p.573). Cooper & Torczon 'Engineering a Compiler' - 2nd ed. (2012) Ch.14 'Optimizing for Parallelism and Locality' is the loop-carried-dependence/distance-vector treatment; 3rd ed. (2023, ISBN 978-0-12-815412-0) reorganized optimization into Ch.8 'Introduction to Optimization'/Ch.9 'Data-Flow Analysis'/Ch.10 'Scalar Optimization' (publisher cites loop-fusion material around pp.379-447), so cite by edition.
recommendations: Implement exactly four exact per-dimension tests in this order and stop at the first independence proof: ZIV, Strong SIV, Weak-Zero SIV, Weak-Crossing SIV; add the bounded-Diophantine general case (a*i-b*j=k with box intersection) only for mismatched coefficients like a[2i] vs a[i]. Skip Omega/polyhedral entirely and say so in the report - for your subscript grammar everything above is EXACT, which is a stronger claim than production compilers usually get to make.

Adopt LLVM's return-convention internally: every test returns 'disproved/independent?' bool and writes refinements (distance, direction bits) into a shared FullDependence-like struct with per-level {Distance: Option<i64>, Direction: {LT,EQ,GT} bitset}. This makes the code mirror the paper and makes unit tests trivial.

Perform ALL analysis arithmetic in i64 (consider i128 for c*i terms and Banerjee-style bounds), regardless of whether elements are i32/f32 - LLVM explicitly widens to 2B+levels+1 bits for this reason; document the choice in the report as overflow-safety of the ANALYZER itself.

Model dependences as a small per-nest graph: node per statement, edge annotated {kind RAW/WAR/WAW, base array, level, distance: Option<i64>, dirs}. Run SCC; a cycle = serial loop UNLESS every cycle edge is a recognized reduction self-loop. Then print 'Loop #N: RAW n / WAR n / WAW n => SAFE/SEQUENTIAL' from edge counts at the target level.

Handle the three canonical teaching examples as golden tests: (1) a[i]=a[i-1]+1 -> RAW dist 1 => sequential; (2) a[i]=b[i]*2 -> no same-array pair => SAFE; (3) s+=a[i] -> reduction exemption => SAFE-with-reduction. Add a[2i]=a[i] (GCD inconclusive, exact box test decides) and a[i][j]=a[i][j-1]*x (level-2 carried) as 2D cases.

Reduction recognition checklist to enforce: single assignment to x per iteration of the form x=x op t or x=t op x; op in {+,-,*,min,max}; no other references to x in the body; seed private accumulators with identities (0,0,1,+MAX,+MIN) and merge after join; propagate final value back. Emit a WARNING (not silence) when x is f32/f64 and op is + or * because reassociation changes rounding; offer a fast-math-style language flag to permit it.
Treat RAR (input) dependences as always-ignorable and SAY SO in the report; many student implementations wrongly block on them.

State in the report that HELIX's SSA form already removes scalar anti/WAW dependences by construction (renaming), so only ARRAY false dependences (WAR/WAW through [T]) can ever force serialization - that is a clean, true observation tying your IR to Allen & Kennedy Ch.3, with privatization/array-expansion described qualitatively as future work.

Bound every test with trip counts: require N=U-L+1 >= 1, clamp/verify source and sink indices against [L,U] after computing distances (LLVM's insight that a single-trip loop cannot carry a '<' or '>' dependence is a nice extra check that catches off-by-one bugs).

Use std::thread::scope with chunks_mut() sized len/num_cpus (std::thread::available_parallelism()) rather than pulling rayon, to keep the dependency story of a course project minimal; rayon 1.12.0 par_chunks_mut is the drop-in alternative if you want work-stealing; compile the kernel with cranelift-jit 0.135.0, finalize before spawning, and pass raw chunk pointers as extern "C" fn(*mut T, usize).
pitfalls: Sign-convention bugs on distance/direction: some texts define d = i_sink - i_source, others (LLVM's Delta = Src-Dst) invert it and then map positive distance to LT; pick ONE convention, write it in a comment, and unit-test a[i-1] (WAR-looking but actually RAW dist +1) vs a[i+1] (dist -1, i.e. a backward 'anti-flow' pattern) - mixing conventions silently flips SAFE/UNSAFE verdicts.

Forgetting loop bounds entirely: the GCD test alone ignores them, so a[i] vs a[100] in a 10-trip loop looks dependent; conversely Banerjee bounds computed with the wrong max index (trip count N vs last index N-1 vs LLVM's backedge-taken count) produce off-by-one independence proofs that are UNSOUND, not just imprecise. A single-trip loop must never yield a '<' or '>' direction.

Treating a PASSED test as proof of dependence: GCD and Banerjee are necessary conditions - passing means 'unknown', failing means 'independent'. Reporting 'dep found because gcd divides delta' is the classic inversion error.

Unsigned/wraparound mishandling: in Rust, debug builds PANIC on i32 overflow while release builds WRAP silently (overflow-checks profile flag), and in C signed overflow is UB (compilers exploit no-wrap assumptions; -fwrapv disables). If your front-end lets index expressions overflow, monotonicity arguments behind SIV distance math break; compute analysis in wider ints and decide explicitly whether HELIX source arithmetic wraps (document it; consider wrapping_mul/wrapping_add semantics or rejecting overflowing constant folds).

Applying separable (SIV) tests to coupled subscripts: a[i][j] vs a[j][i] must NOT be tested dimension-by-dimension with SIV logic as if dimensions were independent - coupled subscripts need the MIV fallback or a conservative '*'; silently misclassifying them produces wrong SAFE verdicts.

Dropping the conjunctive combination rule: a multidimensional pair is independent if ANY dimension is disproved; students sometimes require all dimensions to disprove (over-serializing) or forget to intersect surviving direction vectors componentwise (under-serializing).

Ignoring intra-iteration ordering: for distinct statements you must allow (same iteration + statement order) as a valid loop-independent dependence; for same-statement pairs you must REQUIRE strictly increasing iterations. Getting lexicographic order wrong turns a[i]=b[i]+a[i-1] into nonsense.

Reduction over-recognition: accepting x = x op y when x has OTHER reads/writes elsewhere in the body, when the op chain isn't a single associative fold (e.g. x = (x+a)*b), or ignoring float non-associativity - each silently changes program results. Also remember min/max identity values and post-loop final-value propagation.

Assuming unit stride or known trip counts: guard with a runtime check (or bail to sequential) when N<=0 or when bounds are symbolic and the divisibility/interval arguments can't be made; LLVM adds explicit SCEV predicates/runtime assumptions for exactly this reason (e.g. proving coefficient != 0 before concluding '=' direction in strong SIV).

Alias/base-array confusion: the analysis is only sound because HELIX arrays are values with no aliasing; the moment you add pointers or slices-as-views, same-base-name checks stop being sufficient - note this limitation in the report instead of discovering it as a bug.
Overflow INSIDE the analyzer: evaluating c*i or bound sums in i32 can wrap and flip an independence proof; this is precisely why LLVM widens Banerjee arithmetic to 2B+levels+1 bits.
